# Evidence log

The running record of evidence (news, feedback, primary documents) as it arrives. Append a row each time something lands; tie it to the requirement(s) it affects, give it a trust tier, and note the action taken (revise / validate / no-change). The daily baseline freezes this file, so the evolution of the evidence base is visible across days.

**ID convention:** `E-YYYY-MM-DD-NN` (NN = sequence within the day).
**Trust tiers:** A = primary/authoritative · B = vendor-primary (true but promotional) · C = specialist trade press · D = secondary/aggregator. (See ADR-001 source-trust assessment.)
**Action:** `revise` (changed a decision/status) · `validate` (confirmed an existing one) · `watch` (noted, no change yet).

Paraphrased: GSM-R runs the high-load core to 2026 with special resilience, FRMCS for the surrounding area from ~2030; "aus einem Guss" coordinated equipping of GSM-R+FRMCS+public mobile; vehicle retrofit (Alstom, mid-2021) two-stage (stage 1 antennas/cables/netboxes now; stage 2 modems/filters + SW update early 2030s) at a few €k/EMU; Federal funding of 333 regional EMUs tied to 24 technical conditions; FRMCS ordered for 130 Alstom Coradia Max + 28 Siemens Mireo; RESILIENCE (§3.1): 99.992% BTS availability for ETCS L2oS via 3-BTS loops; 19 BTS failures among ~40 BTS 2018–20 + 2 BSC failures, effects mostly minor (trains pass dead spots, no auto-brake on L2oS, 40 s recovery); a hot-standby dual-layer was CONSIDERED and REJECTED (≈2× cost, detect-fail-then-restart with ops suspended, shared-frequency burden); instead condensed/overlapping BTS spacing + alternating BTS–BSC loop links so a BTS/chain/BSC loss is ridden through within the 40 s timer, doubled min level −92 dBm, tunnel-BTS batteries, prioritised maintenance; SPECTRUM: extended GSM-R 2×3 MHz (15 carriers) below the interoperable base band (2×4 MHz, 19 carriers), FRMCS at 1900 MHz, worst-case spec to meet TSI CCS (~2027), FRMCS planning on MORANE2 basis from ~2026/27; TRANSITION: 2030–2035 GSM-R (900 MHz) as temporary FRMCS fallback, then after switch-off its 900 MHz band reused to ~double FRMCS coverage; candid Hemmschuh = shortage of qualified rail-specific planners/approvers, EBA approval ≥1 yr | Technical journal (operator-authored, primary) | SIGNAL+DRAHT (DVV Media Group), 5/2025 — authored by the DKS project team (DB / BW Ministry); paraphrased, not quoted (copyrighted) | A/C | R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R7, R13 | validate | Tier A/C: first-hand operator/practitioner account of DB's own live FRMCS pilot (primary, A) carried in a technical journal with mild project-advocacy framing (C); not vendor PR. R3/R4: primary evidence of DB's radio-ACCESS resilience (loop redundancy + overlapping coverage so no single BTS/BSC stops ops; real degraded-mode behaviour) — but ACCESS-LAYER, node-scoped; it does NOT address the national-core SPOF the 23 Jun 2026 outage exposed (E-15/-18), and DB explicitly chose AGAINST a hot-standby dual-layer → R3 stays open, R4 stays the PoC objective (informs, not closes). Substantiates R13 (funded 333-EMU retrofit; cheap two-stage retrofit; personnel/approval bottleneck = the feasibility risk). Corroborates R5 (ATO GoA2/ETCS L2oS; ATO data via public mobile until FRMCS) and R7 (extended GSM-R band, 1900 MHz, TSI CCS, MORANE2). | E-2026-06-28-06 | 2026-06-28 | CSM-RA significant-change framework VERIFIED vs primary law (EUR-Lex) — Commission Implementing Reg (EU) No 402/2013 (Common Safety Method for risk evaluation & assessment), under the Railway Safety Directive (2004/49/EC Art 6(4); now recast as Dir (EU) 2016/798). Confirms the open-letter framing (E-2026-06-28-05) is ACCURATE: Art 4(2)(a)–(f) sets exactly six significance criteria — (a) failure consequence (credible worst case), (b) novelty, (c) complexity, (d) monitoring/Überwachbarkeit, (e) reversibility, (f) additionality (cumulative recent changes); the PROPOSER decides significance by expert judgement (Art 4). If NOT significant → "keeping adequate documentation to justify the decision shall be sufficient" (Art 2(2)(b)), no independent assessment. If SIGNIFICANT → full CSM risk-management process (Art 5, Annex I) + MANDATORY independent assessment by an assessment body (AsBo) (Art 6) | Regulatory (primary law) | EUR-Lex CELEX:32013R0402 (Reg (EU) 402/2013), Arts 2(2)(b), 4, 5, 6, Annex I | A | R3, R4 | revise | A-tier primary-law verification (cf. FRMCS design principles: (1) DECOUPLE connectivity from rail applications — different lifecycles, and explicitly to avoid lengthy re-homologation on changes for safety-relevant apps; (2) max COTS. Transport stratum (5G core/NR + non-3GPP Wi-Fi/satellite) + service stratum (MCX); FRMCS Onboard Gateway maps apps→radios; railways own their FRMCS infra (mandatory in DE for safety apps) + public network as backup/capacity. DB ROADMAP: build own FRMCS from ~2025 → nationwide GSM-R→FRMCS transition ~2035; ATO GoA2 initially on PUBLIC networks (not safety-critical then) → ported to DB FRMCS ~2027; GoA4 over DB FRMCS ~2030+. Standardisation UIC/ETSI/3GPP/ECC; ERA TSI 2022 = first FRMCS version. R&D: Ericsson (5G core/QoS), Kontron (MCX), Nokia (resilience + redundancy RAN+Core+fibre), Vodafone (public fallback for non-safety data). | E-2026-07-01-09 | 2026-07-01 | ETSI TS 103 147 V1.1.1 (2013-06), "Railway Telecommunications (RT); GSM-R Core Network Redundancy" — ETSI Technical Specification (TC-RT; ref DTS/RT-0026). PRIMARY normative standard for GSM-R core-network redundancy. Paraphrased: GSM-R is safety- and QoS-critical, so CN redundancy is needed to cope with MSC single outages — explicitly incl. PLANNED events "e.g. maintenance activities" that cause MSC/core downtime. Redundancy = combination of three 3GPP features: RANflex (Intra-domain RAN→multiple CN nodes, "MSC pool", Rel-5, TS 123 236) for p2p; Coexistence of VGCS/VBS + RANflex (Rel-7); GCSMSC + GCR Redundancy for VGCS/VBS (Rel-11, backup Group-Call-Serving-MSC + synchronized Group Call Register). Mostly 'basic' 1+1 (≤2 MSCs), also 1+N. KEY requirement (§4.2): "redundancy without the need of physical intervention in case of disaster recovery, i.e. AUTOMATIC switchover, NO manual switchover"; backup MSC has same info as failed one; not required to maintain ongoing calls (calls drop, service restores) | Standard (primary — ETSI TS) | ETSI TS 103 147 V1.1.1 (2013); paraphrased, not quoted (copyrighted) | A | R3, R4 (+ R7, PR11, incident-annex) | validate | A-tier PRIMARY normative standard — the ETSI spec for the exact thing that failed on 23 Jun: GSM-R CORE-NETWORK REDUNDANCY. ANCHORS R3 (eliminate central SPOF: MSC pool / 1+1 / 1+N, GCR redundancy) and R4 (fail-soft) in a standards requirement, not assertion. DECISIVE for the incident: §4.2 REQUIRES "automatic switchover, no manual switchover" — the 23-Jun outage (auto-failover did not engage → ~90 min MANUAL recovery, E-2026-06-27-03) is a NON-CONFORMANCE to this ETSI requirement; and §4.1 explicitly names "maintenance activities" as a case redundancy must cover — exactly the 23-Jun trigger. Sharpens PR11 (silent-fault defeats auto-failover) with a normative yardstick. NB era: GSM-R/Rel-11 (2013) — applies to the legacy + bridge estate in service now; the SAME automatic/health-driven-failover requirement carries to the FRMCS 5GC/IMS target. No status change → matrix refs R3/R4; note incident-annex + PR11. | E-2026-07-06-10 | 2026-07-06 | Peleska & Schulz, "Reliability Analysis of Safety-Related Communication Architectures", SAFECOMP 2010 (Springer LNCS; Univ. Bremen AGBS), 6 pp. — peer-reviewed formal-methods paper on the EN 50159 SAFETY-LAYER / "GREY CHANNEL" architecture. (1) EN 50159-2 splits safety-related comms into a SAFETY LAYER (meets a SIL) over an untrusted grey channel (COTS transport, no safety responsibility); the safety layer must detect the SIX message-error threats (repetition, deletion, insertion, resequence, corruption, delay) via the standard defence matrix (seq-no, timestamp, timeout, src/dst ID, feedback, ID procedure, safety code). (2) SAFETY-VS-RELIABILITY: the safe reaction to a detected error is a SAFE STATE that STOPS comms until reset → safe communication REDUCES availability; recovered by adding a reliable transmission service (ARQ) in the grey channel. (3) CAUTION: a NAIVE combination of grey-channel + safety-layer fault-tolerance does NOT necessarily raise overall fault-tolerance (ARQ retransmits may deliver out-dated msgs the safety layer discards) — must be ANALYSED. (4) METHOD: model in DSL CAMoLa → per-fault "mutant" models → UPPAAL timed-automata check A□(SAFE ∧ ¬φ); reliability = P(correct or safe-mutant behaviour over operational period); avoids probabilistic model-checking (state-explosion). WHAT v1.0.0 SPECIFIES (M-level, paraphrased): three-strata architecture (Railway Application / Service / Transport), decoupling as design principle — "future transport technologies will be introduced as FRMCS evolves with no impact on railway applications" (§12.1.1), FRMCS shall interface Railway Applications e.g. ETCS (§5.1.5); RMR SPECTRUM per EC Decision 2021/1730: 874.4–880.0 / 919.4–925.0 MHz paired + 1900–1910 MHz unpaired, 3GPP 5G NR (M), operator implements 900 or 1900 or both (§8.4); BEARER FLEXIBILITY (§12): FRMCS Multipath across FRMCS AND NON-FRMCS transport domains — public MNOs, non-terrestrial/satellite, WLAN, 4G EPS — with transport-domain selection/transition TRANSPARENT to the application stratum (M), infrastructure-configurable rule set (path quality × session attributes), aggregation (O), standards-based (IETF) (M); Multi Access ATSSS-based (M); Intra-RAT incl. RAN SHARING with a public MNO (M); QoS (§14): E2E KPIs at the app↔FRMCS reference point — immediate session establishment ≤1 s / normal ≤3 s (99%-ile), talker assignment <300 ms (99%-ile emergency / 95%-ile other), standardized 5QI set {5,7,65,67,69,76}, ARP 1–8 (M), MC-server-driven QoS signalling into the 5GC PCF (M), predefined defaults when unidentified (M); CYBERSECURITY (§15): defence-in-depth, service/transport strata security functionally independent, GDPR functions (M); MINIMUM SECURITY LEVEL "implemented and applied" (M, Table 8): AEAD_AES_128_GCM (MCX media/signalling, TS 33.180), OpenID Connect 1.0 MCX user auth, 128-NEA1/128-NIA1, EAP-AKA′ + 5G AKA (TS 33.501). WHAT v1.0.0 EXPLICITLY DOES NOT SPECIFY (editor's notes on the face — the gap map): §9 GSM-R INTERWORKING & MIGRATION — EMPTY, deferred to a later version (→ ETSI TR 103 768 / TS 103 792); §10 interconnection/roaming/border-crossing — not addressed; §13 NETWORK SLICING — not addressed; §16 positioning — not addressed; §17 non-functional reqs incl. §17.2 FRMCS SYSTEM MONITORING — header-only, not addressed; real-time QoS monitoring/logging of individual sessions FFS (§14.7.10); §15.2.1 places patching, logging, MONITORING, anomaly detection, incident response OUT OF SRS SCOPE (→ complementary security guidelines) and risk assessments are not covered; §15.3 FFS: multipath/multi-access security, non-terrestrial, FALL BACK TO PMNO AND GSM-R; Table 6 Note 3: experts recommend AEAD_AES_256_GCM for MCDATA as AES-128 "will become vulnerable within the foreseeable lifespan of FRMCS". | E-2026-07-12-04 | 2026-07-12 | Master's thesis (Tesi di Laurea Magistrale in Ingegneria Informatica), Univ. Napoli Federico II, AY 2020/2021 — Francesco Vitale, supervisors Prof. Nicola Mazzocca + Prof. Francesco Flammini: "Run-time Anomaly Detection with Process Mining: Methodology and Railway System Compliance Case-Study", 146+ pp. Paraphrased: a Process-Mining CONFORMANCE-CHECKING methodology (token replay) that validates the RUN-TIME behaviour of an ERTMS/ETCS system against DESIGN-TIME process models (BPMN → Petri nets) extracted from the ETCS SRS — case study: START OF MISSION, Level 2 Full Supervision. A Fitness metric with PER-COMPONENT weights (λ_DMI/λ_EVC/λ_RTM/λ_RBC) both detects anomalies and classifies their SEVERITY and PHYSICAL LOCALIZATION: perfect runs fitness 1.00; DETECTED errors (system rolls forward, e.g. RBC unavailable + 2 retries) 0.93–0.97, severity Very Low; LATENT errors (corrupted RBC/EVC phases) 0.34–0.77, severity Medium — the metric SEPARATES DETECTED FROM LATENT FAULTS from the event trace alone. Fault-injection campaign on a distributed lab prototype (Raspberry Pis + laptop, MQTT pub/sub; DMI/EVC/OB/RTM/RBC components; code on GitHub): RBC unavailability, sensor failure, RBC-connection loss mid-routine, phase corruption; fault taxonomy explicitly includes INTRUSION ATTEMPTS (compromised node → "harder-to-detect, possibly latent" anomalies) vs easily-detected physical interference. | E-2026-07-24-01 | 2026-07-24 | ACM CCS '25 (Shaik, Jaschek, Seifert — TU Berlin): "Uncovering hidden paths in 5G core: Exploiting protocol tunneling and network boundary bridging". Empirical security evaluation of six production-grade 5G SA cores (open-source Open5GS, free5GC, OAI-5G, SD-Core; two commercial PC1/PC2) using Tunneler, a Scapy-based UE-side probing tool. Paraphrased: a compromised UE (commercial smartphone + valid SIM) abuses two MITRE-FiGHT vectors — PROTOCOL TUNNELING (GTP-U-in-GTP-U: the UPF treats the inner GTP header as opaque payload, performs no nested-header inspection, and mis-routes to an attacker-chosen inner TEID/IP) and NETWORK BOUNDARY BRIDGING (user-plane traffic reaches control-plane NFs — AMF via NGAP injection, SMF/UPF via PFCP injection — because N2/N4 IPsec is "often disabled in deployments that assume physical security" and UPFs lack egress/routing enforcement). 7 vulnerabilities + 6 undocumented weaknesses across misrouting logic, insufficient validation, and spec ambiguity. Identifier weaknesses: 32-bit TEID often uses only low 16 bits + sequential allocation → enumerable <11 s at 1000 pps; Open5GS SEID uses only 12 bits (space 4096, scanned <9 s); NO core rate-limited error responses. Three validated attacks: A1 direct UE-to-UE data injection (bypasses the external data network + network-layer defences); A2 charging fraud via reflection (spoofed victim uplink TEID; amplified DNS reflection consumed ~46 KB on the victim with no attacker downlink billed); A3 full traffic interception / Person-in-the-Middle via a rogue gNodeB registered through NGAP boundary-bridging — "existing 5G security mechanisms [mutual auth, encryption, integrity, downgrade prevention] do not defend against PITM". DoS: SD-Core crashed on malformed PFCP (manual restart); Open5GS/free5GC terminated all sessions under PFCP session-table saturation → forced re-registration. Mitigations proposed: bind SEID to source identifier (as TEID-IP already is), mandate full identifier entropy, specify PFCP handling of empty/malformed messages, cap GTP-U encapsulation at one layer (inspect first 64 bytes), rate-limit control-plane messages + per-IP PFCP session quotas, deny-list N3→N4/internal re-entry, IPsec on N2/N4. Responsibly disclosed to core maintainers + industry bodies; all tests lab-isolated (Faraday cage) | Academic research (peer-reviewed — ACM CCS, top-tier security venue) | Altaf Shaik, Robert Jaschek, Jean-Pierre Seifert (TU Berlin); ACM CCS '25, Taipei, Oct 2025; file "Uncovering_hidden_paths_in_5G_core...pdf", Download folder | A | R14 (+ R5 target-core surface; R3/R4 DoS/availability) | validate | A: peer-reviewed primary empirical research at a top-tier venue, named academic authors, first-hand evaluation of six real 5G cores — strongest evidence class in the log for the FRMCS-target attack surface, above the unrefereed Vitale thesis (E-2026-07-12-04) on rigour. TIER CAVEATS: (1) CAMERA-READY/preprint — DOI (10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn) + ACM ISBN are PLACEHOLDERS, no final page numbers → capture the final ACM DL version before load-bearing external citation; (2) 5G-GENERIC, NOT RAIL-SPECIFIC — six open-source/anonymised-commercial cores, none FRMCS/rail-procured; applicability to FRMCS is by INHERITANCE (FRMCS = 3GPP 5G SA, same UPF/GTP-U/NGAP/PFCP surface), an inference not a rail test; (3) lab-isolated + responsibly disclosed — some cores may already be patched. WHY VALIDATE (not revise): strengthens R14's secure-by-design threat basis with hard primary evidence; does NOT flip a status — R14 stays Open, ADR-012 stays Proposed. SUBSTANTIATES the CSO-validation (cso-validation-2026-07-21.md): §1 "5G SBA API exploitation, slice mis-isolation" now backed by empirical UPF/NGAP/PFCP exploitation; §3 zone/conduit — NBB is EMPIRICAL PROOF the control/user-plane boundary (candidate zone Z2 FRMCS core) is bridgeable under weak routing enforcement, a conduit-boundary failure not a theoretical one; PR19 candidate (DoS on FRMCS SBA surfaces) — SD-Core crash + session-table saturation are concrete instances (R3/R4 bearing); A3 PITM defeating mutual-auth/encryption is the security analogue of the silent-fault lesson (standard 5G controls do not self-report this compromise). The Agency's formal Article-12 deliverable to the European Commission: mandated by CCS TSI 2023/1695 Art 12 to analyse (by 1 June 2024) "how to PHASE OUT the checks to prove the technical compatibility of on-board units with different ERTMS trackside implementations and to achieve harmonisation of engineering and operational rules for the Single European Rail Area". Paraphrased key findings: ESC (ETCS System Compatibility) + RSC (Radio System Compatibility) were introduced (amendment 2019/776 of CCS TSI 2016/919) as a TRANSITIONAL measure to instil compatibility confidence, but the large number of ESC/RSC types + multitude of checks now cause ADDITIONAL COST, LONGER PROJECT DURATION and FRAGMENTATION of the ERTMS landscape, sometimes conflicting with the EC verification process. Evidence: of tested ESC types, <10% reported actual train-track incompatibilities; most issues are PRODUCT NON-CONFORMITIES, misinterpretation of requirements, or trackside/on-board design incompatibilities — fix is usually an on-board config update. But the sector does NOT agree ESC can be quickly phased out (strong disagreement with "subsystem certificates are sufficient" and "current maturity allows removal") → no consensus, no straightforward phase-out; a stepwise action plan is needed. 10 RECOMMENDATIONS (short/med/long): (1) dedicated Working Group; (2) harmonized ESC content definition; (3) ESC-definition guideline for IMs; (4) HARMONISED TRACKSIDE ENGINEERING RULES (ERJU System Pillar SP OD working on operational harmonisation); (5) review CCS-TSI conformity-assessment requirements (NoBo §6.3 tables); (6) better ESC coverage by SUBSET-076; (7.1) spec-error-correction via Agency questionnaires (CCS TSI §7.2.10); (7.2) removal of partial-fulfilment clause (transition until ≥2030, Appendix B Table B1.2 line 16); (8) strengthen NoBo/AsBo focus on product deviations; (9) continuous training; (10) CCS national-rules cleaning-up. Ranked key enablers for phase-out: (1) more harmonisation in ERTMS trackside engineering; (2) fully CCS-TSI-compliant ERTMS ICs; (3) full application of the error-correction process; (4) harmonised track-train integration test spec; (5) ERTMS-IC authorisation process | Agency primary report (EU Agency for Railways; formal CCS-TSI Article-12 deliverable to the European Commission; recommendations = analysis/proposals, not binding) | ERA — 2024-REP-Art.12_CCS_TSI V2.0 (era.europa.eu); file "2024-rep-art.12_ccs_tsi_v2.0_0.pdf", Download folder | A | R7 (+ R6 check-/re-qualification-burden reduction; R2 partial-fulfilment 2030 transition) | validate | A — PRIMARY: an official EU-Agency-for-Railways report, named drafters/validators/approvers, versioned (V2.0), the Agency's FORMAL Article-12 deliverable to the European Commission — same source class as the ERA ESC/RSC register (E-2026-07-25-04) and MORANE-2 (E-2026-07-02-15). CAVEATS: (1) it is ANALYSIS + RECOMMENDATIONS, explicitly a "starting point for further discussions", NOT binding regulation — the 10 recommendations are proposals, not enacted requirements (mark as ERA position, not law); (2) V2.0 dated 03/12/2024 (~1.5 yr old) — verify whether the Commission has acted / a later revision exists before load-bearing use; (3) subject is ETCS + GSM-R-radio compatibility; FRMCS is not the topic (RSC-radio only, Annex 5). VALIDATES R7 (interoperability + CCS-TSI conformance, Accepted · ADR-001) with STRATEGIC context the type-register (E-04) lacks: the CCS-TSI compatibility regime FRMCS conformance sits within is itself TRANSITIONAL and formally slated for PHASE-OUT toward harmonised trackside engineering — "conform to CCS TSI" is conformance to a moving, self-reforming target, and the Single-European-Rail-Area endgame is harmonised engineering rules (ERJU System Pillar SP OD), not perpetual per-line compatibility checks. STRONG BEARING on R6 (don't re-qualify ETCS on every transport change, Accepted · ADR-001): the entire report is about REDUCING the compatibility-check burden — and its evidence sharpens R6, because <10% of tested ESC types found real incompatibilities while most "issues" were product non-conformities / spec-misinterpretation → the re-qualification burden R6 guards against is largely catching product/interpretation defects, not genuine transport incompatibilities, which is the case FOR the OBapp/gateway-decoupling + harmonisation direction (recs 4/5/6/8, error-correction process, SUBSET-076). LIGHT BEARING on R2 (coexistence): the partial-fulfilment-clause removal has a transition until ≥2030 (Appendix B Table B1.2 line 16) — a dated marker in the same decade-long window as the GSM-R→FRMCS coexistence. Paraphrased: §1 GSM-R rollout retrospective — UIC spec 1996, 32 European railways committed 1997; Germany ~a decade to deploy (~24,000 km equipped, ~7,000 sites, ~3,000 km fibre, ~8,300 vehicles converted, ~32,000 regulatory approval acts, ~50,000 staff trained, with Quattron support). §2 FRMCS = 5G-based (5G preferred over LTE/4G for ATO low-latency/localization); possible sharing of commercial 5G infrastructure + passenger-5G synergies in passive infra; FRMCS requirement set (marketable/vendor-independent-interoperable products, long-term support, flexible certification, availability ≥ GSM-R, resistance to interference AND EXTERNAL ATTACKS, robust durable elements, seamless ETCS voice+data migration); UIC 3 working groups (Functions / Architecture & Technology / Spectrum); UIC schedule forecast — FRMCS specs+validation by 2024, first TSI renewal 2022, second TSI end-2024. §3 FIVE KEY CHALLENGES: (1) implementation strategy ("think from the end forwards", incremental not big-bang, FRMCS-compatibility as vehicle network-access criterion; commercial-network use via network slicing "somewhat doubtful from the point of view of railway safety"); (2) infrastructure rollout (robust FRMCS core installed+tested first, then network parts; early certification/approval-authority involvement); (3) vehicle rollout & terminal procurement (retrofit planning; distinguish vehicle-fixed vs PORTABLE terminals — portables procured LATE to avoid obsolescence); (4) service migration (CS→PS; all app interfaces need adaptation + new certifications; ETCS/ATO + emergency/group/location-dependent calls re-certified per local config); (5) personnel qualification (parallel operation risks "cannibalisation" of GSM-R staff). §4 early PROGRAM STRUCTURE (sub-programs + steering/program committees incl. external stakeholders). | E-2026-07-26-03 | 2026-07-26 | ETSI TS 103 066 V1.1.2 (2012-04), "Railway Telecommunications (RT); Rel-4 Core Network requirements for GSM-R" (ref RTS/RT-00019; keywords BICC, R-GSM; produced by ETSI TC Railway Telecommunications). PRIMARY normative ETSI Technical Specification describing the Rel-4 Core Network architecture — the Bearer Independent Core Network (BICN) — for OPTIONAL application on GSM-R railway networks. Paraphrased: legacy GSM-R CN relies on Rel-99; this TS specifies the Rel-4 BICN as an OPTIONAL evolution (explicitly "does NOT mandate Rel-4 to become the reference architecture for railways — baseline remains Rel-99"), CS-DOMAIN only. Rel-4 BICN concept: the MSC entity SPLIT into an MSC-Server (signalling only) + a CS-MGW (Circuit-Switched Media Gateway, user data) via the Mc reference point (GMSC likewise → GMSC-Server + CS-MGW; Nc between servers, Nb between media gateways; BICC = Bearer Independent Call Control) — enabling bearer-INDEPENDENT core transport (ATM or IP). Covers reference architecture (Rel-99 + Rel-4), interfaces (A/B/C/D/E/F/G + Mc/Nc/Nb), legacy procedures, legacy services (GSM basic, VGCS, VBS, supplementary) and §7.3 RAILWAY-SPECIFIC services: Confirmation of High Priority Call (REC), Functional Addressing, Location Dependent Addressing, presentation of functional numbers, Railway Emergency Call. It is also the seam that makes DB InfraGO's REGIONALLY-SPLIT MULTI-VENDOR estate work — the Nokia (south) / Siemens+Huawei (north) BSS meeting the Kapsch/Kontron Rel-4 core (E-2026-06-29-02 C; finding-dbinfrago-rel4-core-architecture.md) all interoperate across this standardised A-interface. So it grounds R7 (interoperability, Accepted · ADR-001) at the essential-pinned-spec level, and R8/PR7 (the standardised seam is what ENABLES the multi-vendor estate — interoperability as the counterweight to lock-in). ALSO relevant to the FAILOVER-TRIGGER question (DIAG-009): the BSSMAP RESET procedure + SCCP connection management here are the A-interface-level failure-RECOVERY machinery at the BSS↔core seam (recovery after failure, not the failover trigger itself). LIGHT R3: the A-interface is the BSS↔core connection in the core-architecture picture (equipment-map §4/§5). | E-2026-07-26-11 | 2026-07-26 | ETSI TS 103 764 V1.1.0 (2025-11), "Rail Telecommunications (RT); Future Railway Mobile Communication System (FRMCS); System Architecture" (FINAL DRAFT, submitted for ETSI Vote phase / SRdAP; ref DTS/RT-0082; ETSI TC Railway Telecommunications; 26 pp). PRIMARY normative ETSI spec defining the FRMCS high-level SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (on-network mode). Paraphrased: two strata inside the FRMCS System — SERVICE STRATUM (centred on the 3GPP Mission-Critical Communications (MCX) framework; decouples applications from transport) + TRANSPORT STRATUM (connectivity, mobility, QoS, policy, auth); the RAILWAY APPLICATION STRATUM is explicitly OUTSIDE the FRMCS architecture. Key principle #1: "maximizing the decoupling between the strata to facilitate independent evolution of the Transport and/or Service Stratum without mandating an evolution of the Application Stratum". Components (ch5): FRMCS Domain (Transport Domain + Service Domain), On-Board FRMCS, FRMCS-capable Handheld, FRMCS-capable Object, FRMCS Trackside Gateway, On-Board + Infrastructure FRMCS Multipath Functions, EIRENE (GSM-R-based) System, Non-EIRENE non-FRMCS System. Reference points: OBapp (on-board app), TSapp (trackside app), TSctrl (controller); Local Binding for authentication; tight-coupled (standard 3GPP MCX reference points) vs loose-coupled (OBapp API) application modes. Four APPLICATION TYPES (from UIC FRMCS SRS): I interoperable-IM (ATP/ATO/REC/driver-controller voice), II non-interoperable-IM, III interoperable-RU, IV non-interoperable-RU (e.g. TCMS). Modularity: stand-alone / interconnected international network / GSM-R-interworking / non-EIRENE-non-FRMCS deployments. Procedures (ch6): FRMCS Start/Close of Operation, inter-FRMCS-Domain transitions (per app Type), GSM-R↔FRMCS Domain transition. Cybersecurity (§4.2.5): multi-layered across Transport + Service Strata; at the periphery the OBapp/TSapp reference points (UIC FFFIS-7950) require Local Binding establishing a secured TLS-backed mutually-authenticated control-plane link. IP addressing/routing ch8. Normative refs: TS 103 765-1/-2/-3/-4 (Building Blocks: Transport/Service/On-Board/Trackside), TS 103 792 (GSM-R interworking); informative: UIC FRMCS FFFIS-7950, FIS-7970, SRS, ETSI TR 103 791 (terminology) | Standard (primary — ETSI TS; final draft, current) | ETSI TS 103 764 V1.1.0 (2025-11), DTS/RT-0082 (etsi.org); file "ts_103764v010100va.pdf", Download folder | A | R6 (strata decoupling — the core FRMCS architecture principle) (+ R5 MCX service layer; R2 GSM-R interworking/domain transition; R7 inter-FRMCS-domain interoperability; R4 FRMCS Multipath / multi-bearer; R14 multi-layered cybersecurity + Local Binding/TLS) | validate | A — PRIMARY, CURRENT normative standard: an ETSI TC-RT Technical Specification (DTS/RT-0082, 2025-11) — the FIRST and most current primary FRMCS SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE spec in the repo, same source class as TS 103 147 / EIRENE / the FRMCS SRS (E-2026-07-12-02). PUBLISHED AS V1.1.1 (2026-01): the released edition of this V1.1.0 final draft is now on file (ETSI TS 103 764 V1.1.1, published, 26 pp — same structure) — draft caveat RESOLVED; cite V1.1.1 as the published edition (third-digit publication bump). THE NORMATIVE REALIZATION OF ADR-001's TARGET ARCHITECTURE: everything ADR-001 chose appears here as the actual ETSI FRMCS spec — Service(MCX)/Transport strata split with the Application Stratum OUTSIDE the system (= R6 gateway-decoupling, stated as architecture principle #1 "maximizing decoupling between strata"), OBapp/TSapp reference points, tight-vs-loose-coupled app modes, FRMCS Multipath (R4), GSM-R interworking + GSM-R↔FRMCS domain transition (R2), multi-layered cybersecurity + Local Binding/TLS (R14). STRUCTURE (ToC): railway system overview (asset model, physical-architecture model, high-level ZONE model); cybersecurity within the railway application lifecycle; system definition + initial risk assessment (ZONES & CONDUITS breakdown); detailed risk assessment (SL-T derivation, countermeasures from 62443-3-3); cybersecurity requirements (system security requirements + foundational classes); cybersecurity ASSURANCE + system acceptance (cybersecurity case, verification, validation, INDEPENDENCE); OPERATION/maintenance/disposal (vulnerability management, SECURITY PATCH MANAGEMENT incl. "vulnerability and outage time during system update, maintenance phase", Fig 15-16); Annexes — handling conduits (A), handling LEGACY systems (B), cybersecurity design principles (C), SAFETY AND SECURITY (D), risk-acceptance methods (E), railway architecture & zoning (F), deliverables (G). THE EU-INSTITUTIONAL STATEMENT OF THE INTERCONNECT-SIGNALLING PROBLEM — the engagement's §4a finding, stated by the EU cyber agency in 2018: interconnect = a trust-based "WILD WEST" on protocols "designed decades ago" without security (SS7/SIGTRAN; PSTN-inherited trust model; deregulation multiplied interconnected parties incl. non-operators); risk level assessed MEDIUM-TO-HIGH; attacks "based on the exploitation of LEGITIMATE SS7/Diameter traffic/messages making it very difficult to detect" (= the blending mechanism GTPDOOR later exemplified); "most of the security work has to be done at the PROVIDERS' level" (subscribers cannot self-protect); Diameter (4G) kept "the same interconnect principles" and "has been proved vulnerable"; 5G (then in development): "a certain risk of REPEATING HISTORY… having the same security risks could be extremely dangerous". DOCUMENTED ATTACK LIST: GTP data-session hijacking; O2 GERMANY SS7 mTAN interception → bank-account draining (DE precedent); location tracking; subscriber-profile extraction via Diameter; DoS on an operator; Nordic regulators' joint SS7 recommendations (2015). RECOMMENDATIONS: to EC — "consider revising the current LEGAL LANDSCAPE so that signalling security is covered" + baseline security requirements for providers (2018: NOT covered); to NRAs — national analysis + incident-reporting coverage; to industry/SDOs — "ensure security is covered properly within the new 5G standards". THE MANDATED ERTMS APPLICATION-LAYER SECURITY SPEC — CCS TSI Table A2 index 10d (Reg (EU) 2026/693, E-2026-08-01-11), v4.0.0; the on-board E2E security spec SUBSET-147 references (E-2026-08-01-14). WHAT: interoperable END-TO-END SECURITY for ERTMS data applications (ETCS, ATO, KM = Key Management) over OPEN TRANSMISSION SYSTEMS — the SECURITY LAYER, defined as TLS, sitting DISTINCT FROM the safety layer (Fig 1). CONTENT: §4 Cyber Security Functions — PUBLIC KEY INFRASTRUCTURE (X.509 certs; Root/Intermediate/Issuing CA-RA hierarchy; CRL + OCSP revocation; CMP delivery, RFC-4210/6712), TRANSPORT LAYER SECURITY (TLS 1.3, RFC 8446 + RFC 9150 integrity-only cipher suites; ANSSI TLS guidance), random number generation (RFC 4086), system-wide UTC time service (NTPv4 RFC 5905); §5 REQUIREMENTS — TLS overall + TLS-PKI + TLS-PSK; §5.5 certificate-delivery interface; §5.6 certificate-status-check interface (OCSP/CRL); §5.7 PKI requirements; §5.9 SUPERVISION & DIAGNOSTICS — §5.9.1 FAIL SECURE PRINCIPLE, error reporting/handling. THE LOAD-BEARING PRINCIPLE (§3.1.1.6, paraphrased): "the SEPARATION of safety and security layer is an enabler to keep SECURITY of the communication UPDATED, WITHOUT THE NEED TO RE-APPROVE ANY SAFETY RATING of the application" — the ERTMS-native architectural answer to the CRA-update-vs-safety-case tension (ADR-011); the safety layer (SS-037 Euroradio, for ATP) and the TLS security layer are deliberately decoupled so security patches run on their own cadence. SCOPE (R2 boundary, §3.1.1.11): applicable for PACKET-SWITCHED bearers (FRMCS); NOT applicable for ETCS-over-GPRS (GSM-R legacy keeps the Euroradio SS-037-1 stack). PROGRESS/STRUCTURE/NIS-2-MAPPING update on IEC 63452 — the most current PT-status account on file; context for the CDV (E-2026-08-01-17). SCOPE (broadened vs 2022): whole IEC/TC9 — railway networks (highspeed/mainline/freight) + metropolitan transport (metros, tramways, trolleybuses, fully-automated transport) + magnetic-levitated systems; adaptation of IEC 62443 to rail, taking TS 50701 as input. PT: growth 65 (2022-07) → 138 (2024-10) experts, 4 continents / 20 countries, 15 subgroups, liaison with UITP & ERA (ERJU & UNIFE under discussion), exchanges with ENISA. CD STATUS: IEC 63452 CD Ed1 issued + submitted to NC comments — "improvement and extension of TS 50701"; 228 pp (half normative / half informative annexes); ~66→62 formal requirements; CDV in preparation. | E-2026-08-01-32 | 2026-08-01 | MORANE F 12 T 6001 v3 (29 January 2007) — "FIS for Location Dependent Addressing" (Functional Interface Specification; UIC ERTMS/GSM-R Operators Group + GSM-R Industry Group; ACCESS: Public; approved ERTMS/GSM-R ERIG 29 Jan 2007; 9 pp; COMPLETE TEXT). MANDATED in the CCS TSI Table A2 index 74 (E-2026-08-01-16). THE GSM-R LOCATION-DEPENDENT ADDRESSING (LDA) FIS — LDA = the GSM-R feature where a user dials a SHORT CODE identifying a FUNCTION (e.g., "primary train controller", "electricity supply controller", "secondary controller") and the call is routed to the controller RESPONSIBLE FOR THE TRAIN'S CURRENT LOCATION/CELL. MECHANISM (CELL-SPECIFIC ROUTING): the MSC reads the Cell Global Identification (CGI) from the COMPLETE LAYER 3 INFORMATION message (§6.1.1) to identify the correct controller, and routes the 4-digit short code carried in SETUP's Called Party BCD Number (§6.1.2) — so a driver reaches "the controller here" without knowing their number. The addressing-family SIBLING of Functional Addressing (E-2026-08-01-31). CONTENT: §5 interface description (mobile-originated call setup via cell-specific routing triggered by short codes, on A + Um interfaces); §6 message functional definition (COMPLETE LAYER 3 INFORMATION with Cell Identification/CGI; SETUP with 4-digit short code as Called Party BCD Number). REFERENCES: MORANE FFFS for LDA (F 10 T 6001, Table A2 idx 73 — the FFFS half, NOT on file), EIRENE SRS v15, EN 301 515, TR 102 281, O-2773 enhanced LDA v5.0, GSM 05.08/08.08, 3GPP TS 24.087 (UUS)/24.008. | E-2026-08-01-37 | 2026-08-01 | Eisenbahningenieur (EI) 10/2025, pp. 40-44 (DVV Media Group) — "AutomatedTrain: Konzepte und Systembausteine für fahrerlose Züge" (concepts + system building blocks for driverless trains; subtitle: functional sequence of a driverless preparation run with reaction to a track obstacle). Authors: Oliver Knitter, Julian Hey, Annette Scheel, Jakob Schultz, Henning Voelz — ALL DB InfraGO AG (systems engineers / system architect). THE PROJECT: "AutomatedTrain" — BMWE-funded (German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs & Energy); 9-partner cross-industry cooperation; GoA 4 (Grade of Automation 4 = fully driverless); focus = fully automated PREPARATION/STABLING runs (Bereit-/Abstellfahrten) + automatic coupling/uncoupling; results at InnoTrans Sept 2026; prototype on 2 trains after a 1-year integration+test phase. DIRECT ADR-004 IN-DOMAIN CORROBORATION — the safety-relevant/non-safety-relevant SPLIT: paraphrased, "it is very challenging to realize SAFETY-RELEVANT functions with AI/ML (DIN EN 50716 Annex C.3)"; ZONE 1 (SIL1, highest protection — object in the path within emergency-braking distance) = DETECTION ONLY, no classification, "AI is NOT required" for the safety path; ZONES 2/4 (non-safety-relevant — warning-vest / unauthorized-person recognition) = AI/ML IS used precisely BECAUSE non-safety-relevant — exactly the ADR-004 pattern (AI/ML OUT of the safety-relevant path; safety = detection + SIL; AI = non-safety classification only). ZONE CONCEPT (Tab. 1) with SIL: Zone 1 = SIL1 (emergency brake); Zone 2 = Basic Integrity (beside track, moving toward → service brake); Zone 3 = not-safety-relevant (path beyond brake distance); Zone 4 = not-safety-relevant (unauthorized, report to Leitstelle); reactions = acoustic warning / service brake / emergency brake / report to Leitstelle. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (Abb. 1): AT-System = Object Detection System (ODS) + Vehicle Data Logger (VDL) + AUTOMATIC PROCESSING MODULE (APM-OB) → ATO-OB + ETCS-OB → Fahrzeugsteuerung; APM-OB = central control element, SIL set INDIVIDUALLY PER APPLICATION (not the full SIL-4 of ETCS-OB). HUMAN-IN-COMMAND: departure only after Freigabe durch Fahrdienstleiter (dispatcher clearance). STANDARDIZATION: CENELEC-conform GoA-4 specification documents as basis for future European standardization + Zulassung; modular architecture. References DIN EN 50716/50128/50129/50126/50657, DIN EN 15227, TSI TAF/TAP, DSD KI-MELZS. | E-2026-08-01-39 | 2026-08-01 | ICOIN 2024 (IEEE International Conference on Information Networking) — "An Intent-Driven Management Automation for 5G Mobile Networks" (Yoseop Ahn & Jaehoon (Paul) Jeong, Dept. of Computer Science & Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University, Republic of Korea; © 2024 IEEE; 979-8-3503-3094-6/24; 6 pp; "based on our early IETF Internet Draft" — Jeong is an IETF/I2NSF-active researcher). PEER-REVIEWED ACADEMIC RESEARCH on INTENT-DRIVEN 5G NETWORK MANAGEMENT — an IBN-based Network Management System (NMS) uniting NWDAF + Intent-Based Networking with ML/AI; the RESEARCH-LAYER realization of the sdo-map §1b intent-driven-management pipeline (IRTF/IETF IBN research → 3GPP TS 28.312 "intent document" + NWDAF [TS 23.288/29.520] normative → this). COMPONENTS: (1) NETWORK INTENT TRANSLATOR (NIT) — translates high-level network INTENT → low-level network POLICY (IBN Consumer-Facing Interface ↔ NF-Facing Interface, data-model mapper, NLP for intent translation); (2) CLOSED-LOOP NETWORK CONTROL (CLCS) — dynamically refines the network policy from NF monitoring data; (3) NETWORK AUDIT SYSTEM (NAS) — REMOTE ATTESTATION so all IBN framework elements report their activities, to DETECT SUPPLY-CHAIN + INSIDER attacks (four objectives: verify mgmt system/policy; validate supply-chain/insider risks; assess operational controls; offer corrective actions; audit integrity via remote evidence / blockchain). The IBN Analyzer FUNCTIONS AS NWDAF (TS 23.288/29.520). Built on IETF I2NSF (Interface to Network Security Functions), YANG/YAML, RESTCONF/NETCONF/REST-API per 3GPP; intent constructed per the 3GPP intent document (TS 28.312). Use case: IoT-device data aggregation in 5G. | E-2026-08-02-02 | 2026-08-02 | Singapore IMDA (Infocomm Media Development Authority) advisory — "Compromised GRX Networks Delivers GTPDOOR Linux Malware" ("Advisory for ICM Sectors"; original report published 2024-02-27, updated 2024-03-17; 3 pp). Government-agency cyber advisory RELAYING security researcher "HaxRob"'s GTPDOOR discovery (technical primary = the HaxRob / doubleagent.net writeup, ref [1], NOT on file). GROUNDS THE §4a GTPDOOR EXEMPLAR with a primary government advisory — GTPDOOR = a Linux backdoor targeting systems ADJACENT TO THE GRX (GPRS Roaming eXchange): SGSN / GGSN / P-GW (roaming/interconnect components exposed to public roaming partners, with direct access to the telecom core). RFC 4301 OBSOLETES RFC 2401; UPDATED BY RFC 6040 (ECN tunnelling) + RFC 7619 (IKEv2 NULL auth). SPECIFIES: IP-layer security for IPv4/IPv6 — AH (Authentication Header) + ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload); Security Associations (SA; auth/integrity/confidentiality/anti-replay/traffic-flow-confidentiality); SPD (policy) + SAD (active SAs); TRANSPORT vs TUNNEL mode; key mgmt (IKEv2 default). CHANGES vs RFC 2401 (the edition the SIP paper E-2026-08-02-07 [7] cited): + PEER AUTHORIZATION DATABASE (PAD) linking IKE↔SPD (separates peer-auth from traffic-authz); enhanced/decorrelated SPD-SAD model + multiple-SPD; EXTENDED (64-bit) SEQUENCE NUMBERS; multicast SA longest-match SAD lookup; IPv6 extension-header selector handling; ICMP + Mobility-Header selectors; mandates IKEv2-level features. | E-2026-08-02-14 | 2026-08-02 | ETSI White Paper No. 62 — "A Vision for Communications Security" (running title "A Vision for Telecommunications Security"), 1st edition, May 2024 (ETSI-published, developed in ETSI TC CYBER; NON-NORMATIVE vision/position paper). Authors: Charles Brookson (OBE; ex-Chairman ETSI OCG Security / TC CYBER; 25-yr GSMA Security Group chair; GSM/3GPP security veteran), Laurence Wayne (BT Group; TC CYBER rapporteur for the 6G-security groundwork), Scott Cadzow (ETSI Fellow; TC CYBER rapporteur), Faraz Naim (Accenture UK). A VISION to guide future-network (esp. 6G) security standardization + design. CORE CONCEPT: an INTELLIGENT TRUSTED NETWORK (ITN) — an OVERLAY trusted network imposing a ZERO-TRUST regime across a "NETWORK OF NETWORKS" (4G/5G/6G + satellite/LEO + IoT/LoRa/Zigbee + Wi-Fi + private networks), securing endpoints/users WITHOUT relying on other networks' security. KEY THEMES: legacy protocols (TCP/IP + SS7, "over 40 years old", known weaknesses) must be carried yet cannot be wholly relied on → the ITN overlay compensates; ZERO TRUST (13 principles — nothing trusted by default: no entity/device/identity/protocol/third-party/hardware/software; trust re-established every use; detect+indicate trust failure; DoS resilience; dynamically-reconfigurable endpoint connections to continue through disruption; resilient to classical + QUANTUM cryptanalysis w/ quantum-resistant algorithms); MINIMUM BASELINE SECURITY STANDARD (MBSS) + AUTONOMOUS SECURITY ASSURANCE; end-user/device/customer perspective. LEGISLATIVE context cited (UK-centric): UK Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021, PSTI Bill, ENISA 5G Cybersecurity Standards report. Precedent: Integrated Adaptive Cyber Defense (IACD). Transition to 6G framed evolutionary (build on existing) + revolutionary (the ITN); open-hardware/Open-RAN agility; environmental sustainability. | E-2026-08-15-01 | 2026-08-15 | IEC 61508-2 "Functional safety of electrical/electronic/programmable electronic safety-related systems — Part 2: Requirements for E/E/PE safety-related systems" — **FDIS CIRCULATION DRAFT, doc ref 65A/254/FDIS/c2, dated "IEC: 1999"** (IEC SC 65A "System aspects", TC 65; foreword still carries unfilled `65A/xxx/FDIS` / `65A/xxx/RVD` placeholders → an unpublished pre-publication draft of what became **Edition 1 (2000)**). 69 pp, complete text. THE GENERIC PARENT of the rail EN 5012x series. Paraphrased content: the E/E/PES safety lifecycle in the realisation phase (§7.1–7.9: safety-requirements spec, validation planning, design & development, integration, O&M, validation, modification, verification), functional safety assessment (§8), Annex A (normative — control of failures during operation: diagnostics per subsystem class, watchdog/program-sequence, data paths, sensors/actuators, systematic-failure control), Annex B (normative — avoidance of systematic failures per lifecycle phase), Annex C (normative — diagnostic coverage + SAFE FAILURE FRACTION calculation). LOAD-BEARING CLAUSES for this engagement: **§7.4.2.3** — where a system implements BOTH safety and non-safety functions, "all the hardware and software shall be treated as safety-related UNLESS it can be shown that the implementation of the safety and non-safety functions is sufficiently independent" (i.e. failure of any non-safety function does not cause a dangerous failure of the safety function); "wherever practicable, the safety-related functions SHOULD BE SEPARATED from the non-safety-related functions"; NOTE 1 defines sufficient independence as dependent-failure probability low vs the highest SIL involved; NOTE 2 cautions that co-implementing non-safety + safety functions increases complexity and lifecycle difficulty. **§7.4.2.4** — requirements are set by the HIGHEST-SIL safety function unless implementations of different SILs are shown sufficiently independent. **§7.4.2.5** — where independence is required, BOTH "the method of achieving independence" AND "the justification of the method" shall be documented during design. Also: architectural constraints Tables 2/3 (safe-failure-fraction × hardware-fault-tolerance → max claimable SIL; type A = well-defined failure modes/determinable fault behaviour/sufficient field data, type B = otherwise — SIL 4 needs SFF ≥90% with HFT 1, or ≥60% with HFT 2, and type B at SFF <60% with HFT 0 is "not allowed"); intro sets the claim FLOOR for a single E/E/PE safety-related system at 10⁻⁹ dangerous failures/hour (high-demand/continuous mode) and 10⁻⁵ PFD (low demand); §1.2 designates Parts 1–4 "basic safety publications"; the standard is explicitly framed as the generic framework FROM WHICH application-sector standards are derived | International standard — **PRE-PUBLICATION FDIS DRAFT of a now-SUPERSEDED edition** (IEC SC 65A) | file "iec61508-2.pdf", Download folder; internal doc ref 65A/254/FDIS/c2, "61508-2 IEC: 1999"; PDF metadata: created 2000-08-07, Word source "IEC 61508 Part2-4.0.doc" | A (draft · superseded edition — see caveats; NOT citable as current) | R11 (+ADR-004 FFI/composition; ADR-003 assumption; R9, R10) | watch | **A BY SOURCE, but DOUBLY DISPLACED — hence WATCH, and it grounds nothing citable.** Tier A because it is a primary IEC SC 65A standards document, complete text, first-hand — no intermediary. TWO DISQUALIFYING CAVEATS, both load-bearing: (1) **DRAFT** — this is an FDIS *circulation draft* (65A/254/FDIS/c2), not the published standard; the foreword's `65A/xxx/FDIS` placeholders prove it was never the final artefact. Per the register's own precedent for draft standards (E-2026-08-01-17, IEC 63452 CDV: "DRAFT/not-for-reference, grounds nothing"), a draft cannot carry a safety-case citation. (2) **SUPERSEDED EDITION** — this is the draft of **Edition 1 (2000)**; the current text is **IEC 61508-2:2010 (Edition 2.0)**, which materially reworked exactly the areas of interest (systematic capability, element/"proven in use" routes, the architectural-constraint route 1H/2H). Under the ONE-ROW-PER-SPEC / edition discipline (E-2026-08-01-11/-13), the anchor must be the CURRENT edition — so this row anchors nothing; it is the *lineage*, not the reference. (3) **WRONG LAYER for the CCS TSI** — IEC 61508 is the GENERIC cross-sector parent; the rail sector-specific derivatives (EN 50126-1/-2:2017, EN 50716:2023, EN 50129:2018+AC:2019, EN 50159:2010+A1:2020) are what the CCS TSI Table A 3 cites and what the safety case must satisfy. **THEREFORE IT DOES NOT CLOSE THE PAYWALLED EN 5012x RESIDUAL** — it is the parent framework, not the sector text, and a superseded draft of it at that. WHAT IT DOES DO (genuine, and the reason to log it): it puts the GENERIC-PARENT ROOT of ADR-004's central argument on file in free primary-lineage form. ADR-004 §3 ("Freedom from interference / independence") and its governing composition principle — *"otherwise the agent inherits SIL-4"* — are currently carried as an **ASSUMPTION** resting on UNLICENSED EN 50129 composition wording (ADR-004 action item 4 says so explicitly, and ADR-003's "not high-risk" finding leans on the same unlicensed wording). §7.4.2.3/.4/.5 here state that principle at the parent-standard level in almost the engagement's own terms: mixed safety/non-safety ⇒ EVERYTHING is safety-related unless sufficient independence is DEMONSTRATED; requirements follow the HIGHEST SIL unless independence is shown; and the method AND its justification must be DOCUMENTED. That last point is a direct, if non-citable, corroboration that ADR-004 action item 2 (produce the FFI/independence analysis) is the right deliverable, and §7.4.2.3's "wherever practicable, SEPARATE them" corroborates the Option-A physical-segregation preference over Option-B shared-platform partitioning. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R11 stays *Proposed — load-bearing*; ADR-004 stays *Proposed*; ADR-003's classification assumption stays an assumption; no traceability-matrix status change. The residual is NARROWED in provenance-quality terms only (the generic principle is no longer known solely through secondaries) — recorded as an addendum to ADR-004 action item 4, not as a status flip. **FOLLOW-UP (to make this citable):** obtain **IEC 61508-2:2010 Ed 2.0** (published, current) and, for anything the safety case actually rests on, the licensed **EN 50129:2018+AC:2019** clause text — the sector standard, which is the real target. NOT a security item → master log only. | E-2026-08-15-08 | 2026-08-15 | **ENISA — "METHODOLOGY FOR SECTORAL CYBERSECURITY ASSESSMENTS" (SCSA Methodology), sub-titled "EU Cybersecurity Certification Framework", SEPTEMBER 2021**; published ENISA report, **142 pp**, © ENISA 2021. Authored by a 15-member expert group (Andrukiewicz, Atallah, Bartels, Dörr, Marinos, Michota, Mongay Batalla, Nguyen, Payen, Polemi, **Preneel**, Quemard, Schaumüller-Bichl, Stütz, Ward). **This is the instrument named in E-2026-08-15-06(e)** — the methodology ENISA cited when stating that no sectoral cybersecurity assessment "has been conducted yet for the Railway sector". Paraphrased scope: a **preparatory method for drafting SECTORAL cybersecurity CERTIFICATION SCHEMES** under the EU Cybersecurity Act (CSA), addressing ICT services in individual market sectors, to be run **with sectoral stakeholders before** a candidate scheme is defined. Core principle: establish a sound understanding of the sectoral ICT services/system first — a sectoral risk assessment identifying stakeholder objectives, primary assets and related risks, extended by a "**deep dive**" into the intended use of relevant subsystems/products/services, and by **cyberthreat intelligence (CTI)** on potential attackers, their motivation and capabilities, so security and assurance requirements can be assigned to ICT subsystems/products/services **based on risk**. Structure: §4 sectoral systems in the CSA context; §5 consistent definition of risk/security/assurance — incl. **CSA meta-risk classes** (a common approach to scaling risk), **using ATTACK POTENTIAL to select security and assurance requirements**, risk-based **common security levels (CSL)**, the **common assurance reference concept**, and §5.7 "**triggers for reactions to unexpected events**"; §6 implementation as four workflows — **A** context establishment & business-layer assessment, **B** primary-asset-layer assessment, **C** assessment of supporting assets, **D** supporting-asset **gap analysis**; §7 mapping to security-problem definition / assurance levels / security levels; §8 definition and application of **common controls** (+ a sample list); §9 **cyberthreat intelligence** — what a threat is, **types of attackers**, characterization of attackers, **estimating attacker potential from CTI**, and steps to implement CTI-based attack-potential assessments. §1.4 "State of the work": the methodology "relies as far as possible on standards and proven concepts", some parts "can be seen as innovations", and — the load-bearing detail — "**the practicality of the SCSA Methodology and its applicability in the area of 5G was evaluated in a dedicated pilot project**", with improvements folded into this version; future steps include enhancing the sample control list and consolidating the §9 attacker-potential methods "after their first practical implementation". This row supplies the missing half of that statement: **the method exists, is published, is 142 pp of worked-out procedure, and had already been piloted — just not on rail.** The gap is therefore not "no method exists" but "**the method was never applied to this sector**", which is a materially different and more actionable finding. FRMCS is 5G SA — so the instrument has been exercised on the very technology family FRMCS adopts, in a non-rail framing. That makes a rail/FRMCS SCSA an unusually low-friction proposition: the sectoral method is proven, the technology substrate is already covered by the pilot, and what is missing is the rail sectoral application with its stakeholders. **CANDIDATE REUSE (method, not evidence)** — several constructs map onto engagement work already scoped: **attack potential** and §9 **attacker characterisation from CTI** parallel the adversary-emulation profiles in evidence-log-security.md (Sandworm G0034, LightBasin, APT28 — all currently analyst-assembled without a formal potential/capability scale); **workflow D supporting-asset gap analysis** and the **common security level (CSL)** construct are the shape of ADR-012's PDE inventory + procurement-clause work (action items 1-2); §5.7 **triggers for reactions to unexpected events** is kin to the detection/alerting thread (R12); the §8 common-controls approach parallels the Annex C crosswalk of E-2026-08-15-07. Record these as **available method**, not as adopted method. **CAUTION ON WEIGHT:** CSA certification is **voluntary** and this document binds nobody — for the engagement the **binding** product-security instrument is the **CRA (Reg (EU) 2024/2847)** with its mandatory conformity assessment (ADR-012 legal basis), and the CRA post-dates this report entirely. Do not let an SCSA framing displace CRA obligations; at most SCSA is a preparatory/voluntary layer above them. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays Open, ADR-012 Proposed, R8 Recommended; no matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UP / OPEN QUESTION worth putting to the client:** has any rail sectoral cybersecurity assessment been initiated since 11/2021 (ERA, ENISA, ER-ISAC, UNIFE, or ERJU System Pillar)? then risk-based — security by default, protection from unauthorised access, confidentiality/integrity of data-commands-programs, data minimisation, **availability of essential functions**, minimise negative impact on other devices, limit attack surfaces, reduce incident impact, "**record and monitor security relevant events**", enable adequate security updates. **Vulnerability handling**: identify/document dependencies incl. **SBOM**; READ: complete text (9 slides) | National-authority conference presentation (primary institutional — the French NSA and the French national cybersecurity agency jointly, named officials) | file "01Policy-1 - EPSF-ANSSI - FR approach on Railway cybersecurity.pdf", Download folder; md5 22988ffd…07ae; 2nd ERA-ENISA Conference, Lille, 01.12.2022 (date confirmed in-document) | A (primary — two national competent authorities presenting their own mandates, collaboration and published position paper; TWO FLAGS: **slide-deck form**, telegraphic and non-normative; **2022 vintage** — NIS-2 has since been transposed, the CCS TSI has since issued as Reg (EU) 2023/1695, TS 50701 has since become EN 50701:2023, and the CRA has since been adopted) | R14/ADR-012 (+ **R11/ADR-004 supervisory competence**; R7 interoperability; R12; R10 competence/oversight) | validate | **A — and genuinely INDEPENDENT corroboration, which is what makes it valuable.** Every other cybersecurity source logged today came from ERA or ENISA (and several from a single event). This is a **different institutional vantage entirely** — two *national* competent authorities, in a Member State, describing their own legal mandates and practice. Where it agrees with the EU-agency material, that agreement carries real evidentiary weight rather than being the same body restating itself. **THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST — (a): THE NATIONAL SAFETY AUTHORITY HAS NO LEGAL COMPETENCE FOR CYBERSECURITY.** EPSF states it on its own slide. This is a **supervisory gap at national level**, and it bites directly on the engagement's central coupling: ADR-012's core principle is that **a security update to live safety-critical code IS a safety-relevant change** — classed, gated and assessed under ADR-011/CSM-RA, preserving Rückwirkungsfreiheit at the ADR-004 boundary. But the authority that supervises the safety case (the NSA) has, at least in France, **no legal competence over the security dimension of that same change**, while the authority that has cyber competence (ANSSI, 573 staff vs EPSF's 106) has no rail-safety mandate. The mitigation on display is *institutional goodwill* — a letter of intent, a joint position paper, board membership, joint meetings — not allocated legal competence. **This is the national-level instance of the register's standing §4a "no owner" pattern**, and it is the sharpest form yet: not a missing standard or an unapplied method, but a missing *legal competence* at exactly the safety-security seam ADR-012 relies on. It should be put to the client as a question about **Germany**: does the EBA hold cyber competence for rail, or does the same seam open between EBA and BSI? (E-2026-08-15-02 records ERA's dialogue with "cybersecurity agencies (e.g. ANSSI, **BSI**)" and "railway safety authorities (e.g. Traficom, **EPSF**)" as two distinct groups — consistent with the split being structural across Member States, not a French peculiarity.) **(c) R5 IS ADR-012's TENSION, NAMED BY A NATIONAL POSITION PAPER:** "implement a reasoned holding in safety condition while minimizing the impact on safety demonstrations" is precisely the CRA-security-updates-versus-authorisation-stability trade that ADR-012 identifies as load-bearing and resolves via one gated change process (ADR-011). An independent national-authority recommendation converging on the same problem statement strengthens that ADR's framing considerably. **(c) R6 + (e) "limited cybersecurity requirement in the coming CCS TSI"** are a matched pair worth carrying: a national authority flagging, pre-publication, that the CCS TSI then in preparation — which issued as **Reg (EU) 2023/1695** — carried only limited cyber requirements. That is a second, independent voice on the same gap ERA's own delegation chain produced (radio security pushed to the FRMCS spec, which omitted monitoring — E-2026-08-15-04 + E-2026-07-12-02), and it is the interoperability-side framing of it (R7). **(d) CORROBORATES THE COMPETENCE/RESOURCE THESIS INDEPENDENTLY:** ENISA attributed low detection maturity to "lack of expertise and resources" (E-2026-08-15-06); here a national NSA reports training **22 of its 106 staff** in two-day sessions and flags "time needed to acquire competencies or to upskill rail experts" as an open challenge. Two institutions, two vantages, same conclusion — the constraint is people, not tooling. **(d) ALSO — INCIDENT ATTRIBUTION WAS NOT A SOLVED PROCESS:** "collaboration on railways incidents to identify incidents linked to cybersecurity" was explicitly **not yet finalized** in 2022. Read against the 23-Jun 2026 outage, where a cyber cause was publicly *ruled out* early (E-2026-06-24-09) while the true cause took days to surface (E-2026-06-27-01/-03), this is a useful caution about how confidently and how quickly "not cyber" can be established — an R12/PR5 detection-and-attribution point, and one to raise gently rather than as a criticism of any specific finding. **(e) MINOR BUT REUSABLE:** small RUs and regional authorities flagged as the weaker tier (relevant to any sector-wide FRMCS rollout, R13); rising certification cost (R8/PR13, ADR-012 conformity burden); SMS-integrating-cybersecurity as an open ERA/NSA question (ADR-012 action 4). **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays Open, ADR-012 Proposed, ADR-004/R11 Proposed, R7 Accepted; no matrix change, no ADR change. **STRONGEST ADR CANDIDATE OF THE DAY, offered not made:** an ADR-012 context note recording the NSA-cyber-competence gap and the German (EBA/BSI) question it raises — say the word and I will draft it. **FOLLOW-UP:** obtain the **2021 EPSF/ANSSI position paper** itself (referenced but not on file; produced with SNCF and ERA) — a national-authority primary on the safety↔cyber link, and the source behind R1-R7. (E-2026-08-15-12). **Aviation's answer to the safety-security seam is a named, adjacent-sector precedent worth putting in front of the client — and it is the same seam ADR-012's "one gate for change" principle and ADR-004's boundary are trying to hold.** Note the honest limit: an aviation *organisational* ISMS regulation is not the same problem as ADR-004's vital/non-vital partitioning of a learning component, so cite Part-IS as an institutional-design precedent, not a technical one. **(b) IS INDEPENDENT CONVERGENCE, NOT NEW FACT — and should be cited only that way.** Every item in the presenter's rail diagnosis is already on file from rail-domain primaries: non-harmonised standards · OT supply-chain maturity (ENISA's "for the OT (safety related) ones, there is a gap", E-2026-08-15-04) · legacy systems (ENISA: "not possible to provide relevant recommendations", E-2026-08-15-07) · distributed infrastructure · awareness/culture and "Safety vs. Security". Its value is that an agency from **another sector**, reading rail from outside, independently reaches the same diagnosis — corroboration of framing, not of fact. Because it is self-described secondary research, **do not cite it as a source for any rail claim**; cite the rail primaries and note the external concurrence. **(c) ADDS A FOURTH INDEPENDENT VOICE ON CAPACITY** — "support organisations to have appropriate **resources** in place" and "entities… have **different needs, capabilities and means**". With ENISA (expertise/resources, worse for OT), EPSF (22 of 106 trained) and Traficom (**~1 person** on railway cybersecurity), the resourcing constraint is now attested by four institutions across three sectors, and the "different capabilities" point matches the FI/FR concern that **small RUs and regional operators** are the weak tier — relevant to R13 (fleet/sector-wide feasibility) as much as to R14. **(c) ALSO NAMES THE CROSS-MODAL CRISIS CASE** — coordination with other transport stakeholders "in case of a large-scale cyber crisis" — kin to the EU Cyber Blueprint's rail-sectoral-mechanism gap (E-2026-07-29-02) and to ENISA's planned cross-modal threat landscape (E-2026-08-15-06(i) → E-2026-07-20-01). **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays Open (ADR-012 Proposed), R11/ADR-004 Proposed, R8 Recommended, R12 Proposed, R1/R2 Accepted. No matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UPS:** (1) **EASA Part-IS** as adopted (Delegated + Implementing Regulations) — the concrete text of the adjacent-sector precedent, and the best available model for integrating cyber into a safety regulator's remit; (2) **ECSCG's Rolling Development Plan** — a working example of SDO gap/overlap management that the rail landscape (ERA/CENELEC/IEC/UIC/UNISIG/GSMA/3GPP, per sdo-mapping) conspicuously lacks; (3) confirm the CRA aeronautical exclusion and rail non-exclusion against adopted Reg (EU) 2024/2847 — already an open follow-up from E-2026-08-15-09, now with a stronger reason to close it. This source is marked TLP:AMBER** ("limited disclosure — recipients may share only on a need-to-know basis within their own organisation and its clients"), unlike the TLP:CLEAR Traficom deck (E-2026-08-15-12). Logging it here is within scope because **this repository is PRIVATE** (verified) and the register is an internal working record. **It must NOT flow into any public-facing output** — the LinkedIn drafts (`current/linkedin-post-*.md`), published papers, or any client deliverable intended for onward distribution — **without confirming the marking with SNCF or the conference organisers first.** Attribute-free, effect-level framing only if referenced externally; do not name SNCF practice publicly off this document. **A by source — and valuable as the register's FIRST ROLLING-STOCK cyber artefact.** R13 (fleet-scale FRMCS retrofit, 16-21k DE vehicles, external dependency · ADR-009) has to date been evidenced almost entirely on cost, approval burden, funding and chipset supply; this is the first evidence of what **cybersecurity engineering on the vehicle side** actually consists of at a major operator — and rolling stock is precisely where the FRMCS onboard segment (TOBA / OB_GTW, R6) will land. **THREE CONVERGENCES WORTH RECORDING.** **(1) "Link the security process with the AUTHORIZATION process" (e) is ADR-012's core principle, stated by an operator.** ADR-012 holds that a security change to live safety-carrying equipment is a safety-relevant change that must pass one gate; **EBA claims exactly that gate** on the regulator side ("authorisation of IT-based railway systems and components", E-2026-08-15-11); **EPSF/ANSSI's position-paper R5** framed the same trade ("reasoned holding in safety condition while minimizing the impact on safety demonstrations", E-2026-08-15-10); and here the **duty-holder** names linking security to authorisation as a strategic orientation. Regulator, national position paper and operator now converge on the single-gate design from three directions — the strongest support ADR-012's central principle has. **(2) "Modular architecture ⇒ easier to patch" (d) is the ARCHITECTURAL answer to the CRA-update-versus-authorisation tension**, and it matches a mandated spec precedent already on file: **UNISIG SUBSET-146 §3.1.1.6** deliberately separates the security layer from the safety layer so the security layer can be updated "without the need to re-approve any safety rating of the application" (E-2026-08-01-15), which ADR-004 already cites as the layering precedent for its own separability argument. Spec-level separation and operator-level modularity are the same move: **design so that the patchable part is not the certified part.** That is a reusable design principle for the FRMCS onboard architecture and for the ADR-004 boundary. **(3) Zones & Conduits on the vehicle** extends the zones/conduits chain the register already tracks end-to-end — IEC 62443 → TS 50701 → GSMA FS.61 (core interior) → **SUBSET-147** (on-board consist network, FRMCS zone separated from CCS zone, E-2026-08-01-14) — with confirmation that a major operator organises rolling-stock security the same way in practice. **THE TWO NAMED POINTS OF ATTENTION ARE DIRECTLY FRMCS-RELEVANT (c): WIRELESS and MAINTENANCE ACCESS.** These are the operator's own priority attack surfaces on rolling stock, and both map onto live threads: wireless = the bearer itself (SIM-SEC-001 radio-layer availability, SIM-SEC-003 GSM-R SIM/modem OTA hijack) and the FRMCS onboard radio; maintenance access = the supply-chain/remote-access vector that EBA/BSI raised as an open question ("can a ransomware attack at a rolling stock manufacturer be safety-relevant?", E-2026-08-15-11) and that the register has otherwise only in enterprise-IT form. **CAPACITY COUNTERPOINT (e):** "internalization of penetration testing competencies" is an operator responding to the sector-wide expertise shortage (ENISA · EPSF 22/106 · Traficom ~1 · EDA "appropriate resources") by **building capability in-house rather than buying it** — the first constructive answer on file to a constraint four institutions have now diagnosed. Worth surfacing to the client as an option alongside the ADR-007 test programme, of which "regularly pentest" and modular-architecture patch testing are natural components. **(d) ASSET INVENTORY & CARTOGRAPHY + CyberCriticalAsset** is operator practice matching **ADR-012 action item 1** (CRA PDE inventory, class by category) — a precedent for how a duty-holder actually scopes it, and a useful counter to NS's lesson that "scoping is difficult" (E-2026-08-15-13). **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R13 stays **Open — external dependency · ADR-009**; R14 Open (ADR-012 Proposed); R11/ADR-004 Proposed; R2/R6 Accepted; ADR-007 unchanged. No matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UP:** SNCF's public methodologies reference (b) is unnamed — worth asking which public methodology the rolling-stock process builds on (TS 50701? IEC 62443-3-2 risk assessment?); and note that the still-unfetched **Masteris** article (blocked, awaiting network policy) is from **SNCF Voyageurs' own rolling-stock maintenance/engineering subsidiary** — the same corporate family and domain as this deck, so the two should be read together when it lands. This gives it structure, membership position, method and a roadmap. **THE LEAD THAT MATTERS — (f)5 AND (g): UIC PLANNED AN "FRMCS SECURITY ASSESSMENT" FOR 2023.** That is the single most directly relevant item in this conference batch for this engagement, and it is **entirely unverified**: whether it was carried out, what scope it took, and what it concluded are all unknown from this deck. If it exists, a UIC-level architecture and project security assessment of FRMCS is **first-order evidence for R14 and for the FRMCS security posture generally** — and it would bear on the gap this register has documented from the other side, where ERA delegated radio-device security into "UIC EIRENE or FRMCS specifications" (E-2026-08-15-04) and the delivered FRMCS SRS §15 then placed monitoring, incident response and risk assessment **out of scope** with §17.2 empty (E-2026-07-12-02). **A UIC FRMCS security assessment is precisely the artefact that would show whether that gap was subsequently addressed at the sector level. Pursuing it is the top follow-up from this batch** — via cssp.uic.org or the named UIC contacts, noting that CSSP appears to be a members' platform, so access may be gated. **(a) IS A POINTED OPERATOR-SIDE STATEMENT ON SUPPLIER BURDEN**, and it belongs with the R8/PR13 thread: the end-user assesses, finds the gaps, and returns to suppliers for solutions — while suppliers arrive with products solving "our problems (**that they have brought into our systems**)". That is the sector articulating, in 2022, the exact market failure the **CRA** was drafted to correct by putting secure-by-design, SBOM and vulnerability-handling duties on manufacturers (ADR-012 actions 1-2; PR13 proprietary opacity / vendor-fix dependency). Useful as the sector's own pre-CRA problem statement, alongside ENISA's 2021 finding that supply-chain elements "do not fall under the same European regulatory framework" (E-2026-08-15-07). **(c)/(d) ARE METHODOLOGICALLY KIN TO WORK ALREADY SCOPED HERE:** an **ASSETS × ACTORS threat heatmap** is structurally what evidence-log-security.md's vector/adversary matrix does (ATT&CK-ICS + FiGHT + MoTIF vectors against Sandworm/LightBasin/APT28 profiles); **SBOM and SOC implementation as named best practices** map onto ADR-012 actions 1-2 and 5; and a **"risk assurance process"** alongside risk analysis is the shape of the assurance argument ADR-004 needs. It narrows the §4a gap a little on the *solutions/assurance* axis without touching the operational-interconnect axis. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays Open (ADR-012 Proposed), R8 Recommended, R12 Proposed, R5/R7 Accepted — nothing here is a result. It also contextualises SUBSET-146 (E-2026-08-01-15): a real, mandated E2E application-security spec exists, but per this deck the subsets' security remit remains interoperability-shaped rather than holistic. **(a)3 IS A DIRECT RISK TO R7, AND SHOULD BE READ AS ONE.** Because the mandated baseline is below what operators need, "some operators now are defining cyber security measures, **which lead to specific solutions per operator**". R7's whole purpose is preserving interoperability and regulatory conformance; here **security is becoming a divergence vector inside a system whose defining property is cross-border commonality** — each IM compensating differently for the same under-specification. R7 stays **Accepted** (the decision to conform to the CCS TSI is unaffected and remains correct), but this is a named, sector-sourced *risk to the requirement*, and it is exactly the risk ESCG exists to close by driving common requirements back into the subsets (b2, g3). Worth flagging to the client as an argument for engaging with ESCG/System Pillar output rather than developing bespoke measures. **(a)3 ALSO ANSWERS ENISA'S LEGACY DEAD-END WITH PRACTICE.** ENISA concluded in 2021 that "**it is not possible to provide relevant recommendations to address the cybersecurity of legacy systems in the railway sector**" and that industry involvement would be needed (E-2026-08-15-07). ESCG is that involvement: it explicitly treats current installations as **legacy systems requiring compensating measures**, runs **separate risk analyses per application phase** (existing / near-future / future, (e)), and produces a **base for a migration plan** and an **ERTMS security migration roadmap** (g). For **R2** — a decade-plus of GSM-R↔FRMCS coexistence, i.e. a decade of running legacy alongside new — this is the first evidence on file of a *worked sector method* for securing the legacy half of a migration, and it is directly transferable in shape to the bearer migration even though its subject is ERTMS. **(c)/(d) GIVE THE ZONES-AND-CONDUITS CHAIN ITS ERTMS LINK, AND A CONCRETE ASSET LIST.** The register tracks that chain end-to-end — IEC 62443 → TS 50701 → GSMA FS.61 (core interior) → SUBSET-147 (on-board consist) → SNCF rolling-stock practice (E-2026-08-15-15). Paraphrased: **(a) FRAMING** — Estonia as "a digital state" on "**NATO's eastern flank**", host of **NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence**, building "the largest infrastructure project in the Baltic region"; the two questions posed as keeping railways functioning as "the backbone of our everyday economy" and ensuring "this backbone does not break under the pressure of **hybrid attacks, cyber threats and sabotage**". **(b) THREAT CLAIMS — see the tiering caveat, these are political assertions:** "attacks against railways are no longer a theoretical scenario… part of everyday reality"; "**over the last two years, Russian hackers have carried out THOUSANDS of cyberattacks on the railway infrastructure of the European Union**" (no source given); four illustrations offered as "different facets of one and the same hybrid campaign" — the **Czech** railway company's "signalling systems… under attack, disrupting the ticketing system"; near **Bremen**, "a railway **cable shaft was set on fire**", causing a full day's disruption Hamburg-Bremen; in **Spain**, "**cable theft** and a technical failure" disrupting high-speed services for two days and stranding "more than 10 000 people" Madrid-Seville; and in **Estonia**, "an attack targeted the **ticketing system** of the passenger rail company". **(c) SATELLITE NAVIGATION AND COMMUNICATIONS — the most technically consequential passage:** "In the Baltic region… the **disruption of satellite navigation and communications**"; Estonia and neighbours have seen "a **sharp increase in GPS jamming**, both in aviation and in maritime transport", with "at times **up to 85% of flights to and from Estonia** experienc[ing] navigation disturbances at some point"; "these disruptions are **increasingly reaching land** as well"; "**precise location information, the correct time and reliable communications are just as critical in RAIL TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT**, in logistics chains and in military planning as they are in aviation"; and the design principle — "**if satellite navigation or communications fail, the rest of the system – including the railway – must be designed so that it does not collapse like a row of dominoes**". **(d) ESTONIAN RAILWAYS PROGRAMME** — electrifying and digitalising the entire core network and raising speeds; "thoroughly upgrading our control, signalling and communications systems"; "a large part of this work means **replacing legacy technology – phasing out Soviet-era systems** and introducing modern, software-based control and signalling solutions"; with the caution that "the more we rely on software and networked solutions, the more important it becomes that **cybersecurity is built in from the outset, rather than bolted on as an afterthought**", and that "**cyber and physical security must go hand in hand**". **(e) RAIL BALTICA** — built with Latvia and Lithuania; "a new main axis for passenger and freight transport", "our economic corridor to Europe", and "from the perspective of the EU and NATO, **one of the key corridors for allied movements on the eastern flank**"; the European Commission's "new development plan for high-speed rail" confirms it as a strategic core route; **target readiness 2030**; and — the operative sentence — "if we are building a railway that must be able, **in a crisis, to carry NATO supplies**, then it has to be designed to withstand cyberattacks, satellite navigation disturbances and acts of sabotage. **Cybersecurity requirements in Rail Baltica have therefore been written into the DESIGN GUIDELINES, the ARCHITECTURE of the technical systems and the CONDITIONS OF THE TENDERS. The same principle must also apply to future maintenance and operation contracts.**" **(f) TWO ELEMENTS BEYOND REGULATION** — *situational awareness*: "we cannot afford to have anyone working in an information vacuum. We must **share information about attacks, incidents and emerging trends BEFORE they escalate into a crisis**"; "hybrid influencing activities do not respect national or sectoral borders, which means our defence must also be **interconnected rather than fragmented**". *People, skills and exercising*: "we may have the best technology in the world, but if, at the moment of an attack, our team is **exhausted, understaffed, or has never practised a similar scenario in a realistic exercise**, that may become our weakest link"; calling for "**more joint exercises**", more cooperation between authorities, companies and cybersecurity units, and "more practical training specifically focused on **industrial control systems and the particularities of rail**". Closes by quoting **Ursula von der Leyen**, in Tallinn: "Critical infrastructure is the new frontier of warfare. And Europe will be prepared."
