The OT slide (c) is written as *oppositions and open questions*, and the speaker's own heading is "the OT world **we (don't) know**" — an honest admission that OT is the less-charted half. **Nothing here demonstrates Zero Trust applied to interlocking, ETCS, or any SIL-4 vital function**, which is precisely the layer ADR-004's boundary governs. So: cite "**Zero Trust works in the context of rail**" as an operator's conclusion about **enterprise and hybrid IT/OT estates**, and do **not** let it imply the vital layer. **THIS ADVANCES THE ZERO-TRUST THREAD FROM VISION TO PRACTICE.** The register holds ETSI White Paper 62 framing **Zero Trust and an "Intelligent Trusted Network" overlay as the design answer** to the interconnect-trust gap — but that is explicitly a non-normative 6G-forward *vision* (E-2026-08-02-14), and GSMA FS.61 supplies **micro-segmentation inside the virtualised core** as deployment guidance (E-2026-08-01-07). This is the first artefact showing an **operator actually doing it on a railway** and reporting that it holds. Together they now form a usable chain: vision (ETSI) → core-network guidance (GSMA) → **operator practice (here)** — though the chain still terminates above the vital layer. **"ASSUME BREACH… MINIMIZE THE BLAST RADIUS" IS THE SAME CONTAINMENT LOGIC AS THE ZONES-AND-CONDUITS WORK**, arrived at from the identity side rather than the network side. The register's zones/conduits chain runs IEC 62443 → TS 50701 → GSMA FS.61 → SUBSET-147 on-board (E-2026-08-01-14) → EUG/ESCG's ERTMS zone model (E-2026-08-15-19) → SNCF rolling stock (E-2026-08-15-15). Zero Trust is the **identity-and-verification complement** to that segmentation-and-boundary approach; both are blast-radius arguments, and ADR-004's freedom-from-interference case is a third instance of the same family — which is worth stating explicitly when the ADR is next revised. **(d) "PARTNERS GET WHAT THEY NEED NOT ALL ROUTES" IS THE CONTROL FOR THE THREAT LOGGED ONE SESSION EARLIER.** E-2026-08-15-25 recorded NCSC-EE naming **service-provider attacks — Ridango (ticketing) and Collins Aerospace** — as a distinct incident class in Estonian transport, i.e. **the operator harmed through a supplier rather than through its own perimeter**. Here the operator states *why*, in one line: "**NIS2D and GDPR: cost of prevention becomes cheaper than risk of impact / fine**". That is the causal link between regulation and spend, from the person who has to make the business case — directly useful when presenting ADR-012's CRA/NIS-2 workload to a client as a budget-unlock rather than a burden, and consistent with NS's operator lesson that legislation "boost[s] existing initiatives" (E-2026-08-15-13). **(c)'s "ONE SYSTEM TO RULE FOR 40 YEARS" IS THE LIFECYCLE TENSION STATED AS SECURITY ARCHITECTURE**, and it independently exceeds UNIFE's "over 30 years" product-life figure (E-2026-08-15-20). Read with R2 (a decade-plus of GSM-R↔FRMCS coexistence) and R13 (fleet retrofit), it is the same problem the register tracks commercially and legally, now framed as an *architectural* one: the security model must span a mixed estate of legacy and modern OT plus modern IT and cloud, for decades — which is exactly why "airgapped and isolated" is no longer available as an assumption. **"MFA ACCESS ON ALL APPLICATIONS INCL. LEGACY" IS A SMALL BUT REAL ANSWER TO A DEAD-END.** ENISA concluded in 2021 that "it is **not possible** to provide relevant recommendations to address the cybersecurity of legacy systems in the railway sector" (E-2026-08-15-07). ESCG then supplied a method for ERTMS (E-2026-08-15-19), the 4th conference showed legacy-train retrofit (E-2026-08-15-22), and this adds the **enterprise-IT limb**: identity controls can be retrofitted over legacy applications. Three partial answers to a stated dead-end, none of them covering vital signalling. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays Open (ADR-012 Proposed); R8 Recommended; R2 Accepted; R13 Open; R11/ADR-004 Proposed — and note explicitly that **nothing here changes the ADR-004 position**, since the vital layer is untouched by this account. No matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UPS:** (1) whether Estonian Railways' Zero Trust programme reaches the **OT/CCS** estate at all, and if so with what safety-case treatment — that is the question this deck raises and does not answer, and it is the one that would matter for ADR-004; (2) the **four-eyes access-validation** mechanism — a concrete implementation of dual authorisation that ADR-011's change-control and ADR-004's human-in-command designs could reference; (3) whether "microsegmentation has never been easier" reflects a specific platform choice worth knowing. a practical approach is needed for **obsolescence**, where a replacement of the same specifications may still count as identical "**provided the replacement does not affect the product's cybersecurity**"; **exception — substantial modification**: if the change affects conformity with the essential cybersecurity requirements or alters the original intended purpose, the spare part **does** fall under the CRA. **⑦ third-party components** — "the key is **contractual control across the supply chain**", with typical clauses listed as: assurances of cybersecurity compliance (**Annex I** essential requirements); obligations to support risk management (**documentation, testing, metrics**); **binding processes for security updates and vulnerability notifications**; **mandatory SBOM** (complete software bill of materials); R13 concerns FRMCS retrofit across **16-21k German vehicles plus ~40k mobile / ~3.5k stationary GSM-R devices by 2035** (ADR-009), i.e. exactly the kind of long-running, unit-by-unit programme this rule bisects. **Consequence for the engagement: CRA applicability must be tracked per vehicle/unit against its placing-on-market date, and the contracts must say so** — the presenter's "clear contractual management is essential" is the right conclusion and is currently nowhere in ADR-009 or ADR-012. **③ "SUBSTANTIAL MODIFICATION" IS THE HINGE FOR THE ENTIRE RETROFIT PROGRAMME — and it creates a TWO-TEST problem the register has not previously identified.** Under ③, pre-2027 products stay out of scope *even when re-supplied later* — **unless substantially modified**. A GSM-R→FRMCS retrofit is, on its face, a candidate substantial modification of an existing vehicle: it changes the communication bearer, adds digital elements, and plausibly affects cybersecurity conformity. **If retrofits count, the retrofitted fleet is pulled INTO CRA scope** — which would be a material, unbudgeted expansion of ADR-012's perimeter and directly relevant to R2's decade-plus coexistence and R13's retrofit economics. **And note the collision:** the same retrofit already faces the **CSM-RA Art 4(2) "significant change"** test on the safety side (E-2026-06-28-06, ADR-011). So **one physical modification may trigger two independent change-significance assessments under different legal regimes with different criteria and different assessors** — safety (CSM-RA / AsBo) and product security (CRA / substantial modification). Worth flagging to the client. **⑥ (⑦) IS ADR-012 ACTION ITEM 2, DRAFTED.** ADR-012 already requires "manufacturer CRA evidence (SBOM, security-update + support-period commitment, CVD contact) as a bid condition". The clause list here is fuller and professionally framed — **Annex I compliance assurances · risk-management support (documentation, testing, metrics) · binding security-update and vulnerability-notification processes · mandatory complete SBOM · authority-cooperation obligations** — and it is directly reusable as the skeleton of the procurement clause, subject to legal review. It also complements the 5G-core-specific control list already attached to that action item (E-2026-07-24-01, E-2026-07-26-14). **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays **Open** (ADR-012 Proposed — its CRA dates are corroborated and its premise better supported, but nothing here changes a status); R13 Open · ADR-009 unchanged; R2/R1 Accepted; R8 Recommended. No matrix change, no ADR change — **though this is the strongest candidate on the board for ADR-012 additions**: the individual-product/December-2027 boundary, the substantial-modification-versus-CSM-RA two-test problem, the tailor-made free-updates deviation, and the drafted supply-chain clause list. "**earliest transparency (status, criteria, risk acceptability, SecRACs…) achieved via MUTUAL AGREEMENT with the customer (asset owner)**". **(d) "WHAT IS A PRODUCT?" — a layered regulatory model, cited as Fig 1 from IEC 63452:** **NIS-2** attaches at the **OPERATOR** level ("CRA product in operation under the NIS2 directive, including organisation — supply chain, incident management…"); **CRA** attaches at the **SYSTEM INTEGRATOR** and **PRODUCT SUPPLIER** levels. Product granularity given as: **systems** (interlocking, rolling stock…) · **sub-systems** (**RBC**, TCMS, platform screen doors…) · **sets of components** (CCTV, door system control…) · **components** (switch, router, PLC, IHM, sensors, camera, recorder…). **(e) FOUR WORKED "PROGRESSIVITY AND PRIORITISATION" EXAMPLES** around the **11/12/2027** line, with a common legend: *CRA compliance not required* (pre-existing component/subsystem/system — "initial baseline") · *CRA compliance "**on the basis of the (system) risk assessment**" — may be used "as is" or with additional mitigating measures inside or around it in the sub-system architecture ⇒ **conditions of use (e.g. SecRACs)*** · *increase of cybersecurity ⇒ "**new baseline**"* · *CRA compliance "**by design**" — designed, developed and produced so as to ensure an appropriate level of cybersecurity* — and, across all four, "**ALWAYS with acceptable risks at system level**". **Example 1**: components, sub-system and system all placed on the market before 11/12/2027 → **CRA compliance not required**. **Example 2**: COMP A and COMP B pre-date the line (no CRA needed for them) but the **sub-system and system are delivered after** → **CRA compliance required for both**; achieved by adapting **COMP B to a new baseline** that raises cybersecurity, letting the (sub-)system reach **compliance at system level**, while **COMP A continues "as is" with additional mitigating measures within it (e.g. configuration) or around it (better architecture — e.g. better SEGREGATION)**, its **conditions of use specified via SecRACs**. **Example 3**: everything after the line → CRA required for all; COMP B compliant **by design**; **COMP A "CRA compliant through CONDITIONS OF USE (Annex 2)"**. **Example 4**: everything after the line and both components adapted to new baselines → both **compliant by design**. **(f) KEY TAKEAWAYS** — expert guidance supports understanding and implementation; "**security-by-design is the key principle for every product development**"; "**communication between manufacturers and railways is essential for transition**". **(g) SYSTEM PILLAR CYBERSECURITY SPECIFICATIONS** — intended to support compliance with standards and regulations, support **interoperability**, reduce development effort and reduce time to market; annotated "**CCS for now and may be more in the future**". **(h) THE PATH FORWARD — open topics listed:** scope of application · **substantial modification** · **tailor made** · **support period** · **spare parts** · **system extensions** · use cases · **SBOMs**; "draft to be approved; validation & publication v1.0 expected for **2026**". The arc is complete and worth stating to a client: **2022 resistance (UNIFE alone) → 2024 joint effort (UNIFE+CER+EIM) → 2025 a standing joint body with a work programme.** Note **Quentin Rivette's third appearance** — SNCF rolling-stock security (E-2026-08-15-15, TLP:AMBER), the 5th-conference agenda, and now representing CER & EIM — a small sector, and a caution when counting sources as independent. **③ (c) CONFIRMS THE ANALYSIS RECORDED AT E-2026-08-15-28 — "SUBSTANTIAL MODIFICATIONS TRIGGER THE NEED TO COMPLY WITH THE CRA."** That row identified substantial modification as "the hinge for the entire retrofit programme" and reasoned that a GSM-R→FRMCS retrofit is a candidate substantial modification. **The sector group now states the trigger flatly.** The consequence for **R13** stands and sharpens: if the FRMCS retrofit of an existing vehicle is a substantial modification, **the retrofitted fleet enters CRA scope**, with the two-test problem previously flagged (CRA substantial modification alongside CSM-RA Art 4(2) significant change) unresolved in both ADR-011 and ADR-012. **"Substantial modification" is on CRSG's own open-topics list (h), so the sector has not settled it either** — which means the engagement cannot simply adopt an answer and should track CRSG v1.0. **④ (e) IS THE GENUINELY VALUABLE PART — A WORKED METHOD FOR A MIXED LEGACY/NEW ESTATE ACROSS THE 2027 BOUNDARY, WHICH IS PRECISELY THE FRMCS MIGRATION SHAPE.** The mechanism: compliance is demonstrated **at SYSTEM level**, not component-by-component; **legacy components may remain "as is" provided they are compensated** by mitigating measures **inside** them (configuration) or **around** them (better architecture, "e.g. better **SEGREGATION**"); the compensation is documented as **conditions of use / SecRACs**; It also answers, from the product-law side, the same problem ESCG solved from the ERTMS side with compensating measures and per-phase risk analysis (E-2026-08-15-19). **⑤ "SecRACs" ARE NEW TO THIS REGISTER AND MATTER TO ADR-004.** Security-Related Application Conditions are the security analogue of the **SRACs** (Safety-Related Application Conditions) that qualify a CENELEC safety case — the documented conditions under which the argument holds. Here they are the vehicle by which a non-compliant legacy component is rendered acceptable at system level. **ADR-004's whole structure is an argument that holds under stated conditions (segregation, unidirectional boundary, human-in-command), and ADR-012 must govern security changes without breaking it — SecRACs are the existing sector vocabulary for exactly that, and the engagement should adopt the term rather than invent one.** The appearance of "better **segregation**" as the canonical compensating measure is further, independent support for ADR-004's Option-A segregation preference. **⑥ (d) CONFIRMS ADR-012's CRA/NIS-2 SPLIT AND GIVES IT A LAYERING.** ADR-012 asserts "CRA — product side… NIS-2 — operator side"; CRSG draws exactly that boundary — **NIS-2 at the operator (including organisation, supply chain, incident management); CRA at the system integrator and product supplier** — and adds a four-level product granularity (**system → sub-system → set of components → component**) with **RBC named as a sub-system** and switches/routers/PLCs as components. **That granularity is directly usable for ADR-012 action item 1 (the PDE inventory), which currently has no agreed decomposition level.** Note it is credited to **Fig 1 of IEC 63452** — the successor standard the register already tracks (E-2026-08-01-17/-20) — so the model has a standards home. **⑦ CAUTIONS ON THE SUPPLIER-FAVOURABLE READINGS.** "**Spare parts are excluded**" is stated more absolutely here than reuschlaw's more careful formulation, which preserved the substantial-modification exception and the "does not affect the product's cybersecurity" condition (E-2026-08-15-28 ⑥); and "**tailor-made products are allowed non-secure configurations and CHARGEABLE PATCHES**" is the plain-language form of contracting out of the free-security-updates obligation. **Both readings favour the supply industry, which co-authors this guidance, and both remain open topics on CRSG's own list (h).** For a rail estate that is overwhelmingly tailor-made and increasingly obsolescence-driven, **"chargeable patches" is a material commercial exposure over a 30-40 year life** — and ADR-012 action 2 should state a position on whether the engagement accepts such deviations and on what compensating terms. **⑧ (h) SHOWS THE SECTOR'S OWN UNRESOLVED LIST**, which overlaps the register's: scope, substantial modification, tailor-made, **support period**, spare parts, system extensions and **SBOMs** — the last being precisely the sufficiency question tmc raised the same day ("what SBOM quality is sufficient?", E-2026-08-15-29). **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION** — but it **closes a flagged risk**: R14 stays **Open** and ADR-012 stays **Proposed**, yet ADR-012's CRA premise, which E-2026-08-15-20 put in question, should now be treated as **sound**. R13/R2 unchanged in status, with the substantial-modification exposure sharpened; R11/ADR-004 Proposed; R8 Recommended. TS 50701?) and how they interact with EN 50129 SRACs — an ADR-004 question. SECURITY item → also indexed in evidence-log-security.md. E-2026-08-01-17 recorded that term correctly; the error entered at E-2026-08-01-20's note, which converted it into a **publication** expectation of "~2027-28", and this row then measured a "two-year move" against that inference. **There was no two-year slip forward: the stability date and the publication forecast were always different things.** What follows below is unaffected — the CDV/FDIS/IS dates are Benoliel's own and the primary confirms the CDV circulation and closing dates exactly.]** E-2026-08-01-17 recorded IEC 63452 at CDV with a **proposed stability date of 2028**, and E-2026-08-01-20 carried a note to "**track publication (~2027-28) to migrate ADR-012 basis TS 50701 → 63452**" — **an inference from the stability date, not a stated publication date**. **This deck supersedes that: the CDV was APPROVED by National Committees in October 2025, with FDIS forecast ~March 2026 and the INTERNATIONAL STANDARD forecast ~AUGUST 2026.** Today is **2026-08-15** — so on the project team's own forecast, **IEC 63452 should be published as an International Standard at approximately this moment.** **The ADR-012 basis migration is therefore no longer a future watch item; it is live, and the first action is simply to check whether IEC 63452 has issued.** Treat the forecast with due caution — the project has slipped before (this register has tracked a Q4-2024 CDV forecast against an actual 2025-08) — but the direction is unambiguous and the gap between "~2028" and "~2026-08" is too large to leave uncorrected in the register's planning. **② (f) IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL ITEM FOR ADR-012: A EUROPEAN ANNEX MAPPING THE STANDARD TO CRA AND NIS-2.** CENELEC WG 26 has already performed a "**common coverage analysis of NIS 2 and CRA regulation**" with "**gaps identified**", and will publish an **IEC 63452 European Annex explaining how the standard's activities and deliverables can be used to COVER CRA and NIS-2 requirements**. **That is precisely the artefact ADR-012 needs and does not have** — a documented route from a rail-sector standard to the two binding regimes, which would let the engagement argue conformance through a recognised standard rather than assembling a bespoke mapping. It also complements the earlier PT deck's **NIS-2 Art-21 → 63452 clause crosswalk** (E-2026-08-01-20) by extending to the **CRA**, and it complements CRSG's draft sector guidance from the same conference (E-2026-08-15-30) — **standard-side and sector-side routes to the same compliance question, converging in 2026.** **③ (d) ANSWERS TWO OPEN QUESTIONS FROM TODAY'S OWN LOGGING.** At E-2026-08-15-30 I flagged as a follow-up "whether **SecRACs** have a standards definition (IEC 63452? TS 50701?)". **They do: SecRACs are named here as a concept IEC 63452 adapts from IEC 62278**, alongside the **threat log** and — significantly — the "**CYBERSECURITY CASE**". A cybersecurity case built on the IEC 62278 (RAMS) lifecycle is the **structural twin of the safety case**, and **SecRACs are the security analogue of EN 50129 SRACs**. For **ADR-004**, whose entire argument is a safety case holding under stated conditions, and for **ADR-012**, which must govern security change without breaking that case, this is the sector's own vocabulary and framework for the safety-security interface — **the engagement should adopt it rather than invent parallel terms.** The explicit inclusion of **CSM-RA risk-acceptance principles** is equally important: it ties the security standard into the same risk-acceptance regime ADR-011 and the CSM-RA change-significance work already use. **④ (e) COVERS THREE PROBLEMS THE REGISTER HAS TRACKED AS OPEN.** "**Handling legacy system**" addresses ENISA's 2021 conclusion that legacy-security recommendations were "not possible" (E-2026-08-15-07) — now a named clause area, alongside ESCG's ERTMS method (E-2026-08-15-19) and CRSG's compensating-measures approach (E-2026-08-15-30). "**Cybersecurity & safety interface**" is the seam ADR-012 and ADR-004 both work. "**Cloud for OT cybersecurity**" bears on the Cloud4Rail / SIL4-cloud thread (E-2026-07-02-27, E-2026-07-02-03) and on the UITP safety-critical-to-cloud item at the same conference (E-2026-08-15-23). And "**flexibility on allocation of some requirements (e.g. who shall perform Risk Assessment)**" is a direct response to the role-ambiguity the register has documented across the FR/DE/FI/BE supervisory divergence. **⑤ (a)'s SCOPING NOTE MATTERS FOR THE PDE INVENTORY: "products (equipment/devices) are OUT OF SCOPE, as 62443-4-1/4-2 apply."** So IEC 63452 governs the **system/integration/operation** layers while product-level security remains with IEC 62443-4-x — which aligns exactly with CRSG's layered model placing the **CRA at system-integrator and product-supplier level and NIS-2 at the operator** (E-2026-08-15-30 (d)), and with tmc's product-side implementation on 62443-4-1 (E-2026-08-15-29). **The three fit together into a coherent stack, and ADR-012 action 1 should decompose along it.** **⑥ SCALE AND LEGITIMACY:** 150 National Committee members across 23 countries and 4 continents, with formal liaison to **UITP, ERA, UIC, ERJU and UNIFE** — this is the sector's consolidated standards effort, not a niche working group, and its **265 pages / 70 requirements / 144 pages of annexes** indicate a substantial instrument. Note also that it explicitly covers **metros, tramways and trolleybuses**, i.e. urban rail — relevant to the scope question the register raised at E-2026-07-25-10. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays **Open**, ADR-012 stays **Proposed** — but its **basis-migration action is now due**, and the European Annex is a forthcoming input it should plan around; R11/ADR-004 Proposed, with SecRACs and the cybersecurity-case concept identified as adoptable vocabulary; R2/R1 unchanged. The register now holds **five distinct handling classes** (RESTRICTED · reproduction-forbidden/proprietary · TLP:AMBER · TLP:GREEN · TLP:CLEAR); **a written handling policy is now overdue and should precede any publication work.** **① THIS IS THE CLOSEST EXTERNAL MATCH TO ADR-004 THE REGISTER HAS FOUND, AND IT ARRIVES VIA A STANDARD.** ADR-004's boundary is: the advisory domain may **read** vital-domain state but **cannot write** into the vital path; the preferred mechanism is a **data diode / unidirectional gateway** on the read path; and freedom-from-interference is argued by **segregation**. **(h) states the same rule from the IEC 63452 side**: telemetry and monitoring data flowing **out of OT to the cloud should be UNI-DIRECTIONAL**, while control signals flowing **into OT must be filtered, authenticated and monitored**. **(i) then formalises it as a three-state directionality matrix per zone pair — "+" bidirectional, "R" read-only enforced by data diodes, "-" prohibited — which is precisely the notation ADR-004's boundary design lacks.** **Recommendation: adopt the communication-matrix/directionality-rule construct in ADR-004's detailed design (action item 1), citing IEC 63452 Annex K rather than this restricted deck.** **② (d) IS THE MOST QUOTABLE ARGUMENT IN THE CORPUS FOR THE ENGAGEMENT'S OWN THESIS.** "**There is no reason why for Safety, the discipline relies on deterministic engineering methodology, while we often tolerate qualitative approaches for Security**" — and the corollary that whenever a **safety instrumented function** is involved, security measures should **meet or exceed the SIL** (SL3/SL4). ADR-004's entire structure rests on determinism: a deterministic SIL-4 kernel, with non-deterministic learning components excluded because they cannot carry SIL-4. **UITP is making the mirror-image argument on the security side, and the two compose: if security measures protecting a SIF must be deterministic and SL-matched, then a non-deterministic component cannot sit inside that protection perimeter either.** That is independent, sector-level support for ADR-004's exclusion of learning agents from the vital domain — arrived at from security engineering rather than safety composition. **③ "SYNCHED SAFETY AND SECURITY CASES" AND THE SIGNED-OFF SECURITY CASE ARE THE MISSING VOCABULARY.** (a) frames the report's scope as **building synchronised safety and security cases**; (d) names IEC 63452's "great contribution" as a **security case signed off by security experts, with deviations recorded and reviewed during O&M**. (E-2026-08-15-29); DP33 supplies two criteria — **automatically generatable and machine-readable**. **⑤ THE CLOUD RISK FRAMING (B-TIER, BUT SOUND) BEARS ON THE CLOUD4RAIL THREAD.** "**The cybersecurity risk doesn't disappear miraculously with a cloud-enabled architecture — it is just shared between different stakeholders, adding complexity**" is the security-side statement of the same problem the register tracks on the safety side: DB InfraGO's Cloud4Rail direction of untrusted COTS virtualisation plus a certified application-level safety layer (E-2026-07-02-27), and the SIL4-Cloud separation-kernel work with its unresolved dynamism and time-sync residuals (E-2026-07-02-03). **Vector ② (bottom-up) is the one to note for this engagement**: it runs from a component at a PLC up through **VOBC, onboard network and the TRAIN-TO-GROUND NETWORK** into the cloud — i.e. **the bearer is in the attack path**, which is the FRMCS-relevant limb and a candidate SIM-SEC vector. Vector ③ (datacentre HVAC/power shut-down) is a **non-cyber-looking availability attack on a hosting facility** — kin to R3/R4's single-point-of-failure concern and to the 23-June lesson that availability can be lost without any attack at all. **⑥ CAUTIONS.** The report is **unreleased**, so its principles are not yet a sector position; the SL-C ≥ SIL recommendation is explicitly the **committee's belief** ("the UITP cyber committee believes"), not a normative requirement, and the deck concedes lowering security measures "is tolerated"; and the vendor conflict at (j) means "hardware enforced protection" should be evaluated on its merits against alternatives, not adopted because it appears in this deck. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** **R11 stays Proposed — load-bearing · ADR-004**, and ADR-004's status is unchanged: this is strong *design-basis* support for the unidirectional boundary and the determinism argument, but it produces none of the **verifying** evidence ADR-004 action items 2, 4 and 5 require (FFI/independence analysis, clause-verified standards, ISA/NoBo assessment). R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed; R3/R4 unchanged; R12 Proposed. The stated complementarity: *EBIOS RM* is "a practical, ready-to-use methodology" with "a neat and elegant way to draw **attack scenarios**", but "complex systems lead to complex scenarios, and difficulty to comprehend the global picture"; *62443 / TS 50701* offer "a complete corpus… defining **Security Levels & Foundational Requirements**" and the "concept of **zones & conduits** refining a whole system into smaller parts, **ideal for handling complexity**", but give "limited information on practical application on detail risk assessment" and "**no representation of attack path scenarios**". **(e) THE STRUCTURE — EBIOS RM's five modules with IEC 62443 "ZCR" steps interleaved:** *Module 1* scope, impact assessment, security baseline (scope · stakeholders · context · inventory · **feared events** · security baseline) + **ZCR 1 identify the system**; *Module 2* threat sources (risk origins & target objectives · **attacker view vs defender view**); *Module 3* ecosystem & strategic scenarios (threat vectors & interested parties · strategic scenarios) + **ZCR 2 initial risk assessment**, **ZCR 3 partition into zones & conduits**; *Module 4* operational scenarios (initial risk assessment · **zones definition** · detailed risk assessment — overview, in each zone, consolidation) + **ZCR 4 does initial risk exceed tolerable risk? ⇒ ZCR 5 detailed risk assessment**; *Module 5* risk treatment (**security level target** · residual risks · treatment plan · achieved risks) + **ZCR 6 document risks and requirements**, **ZCR 7 ASSET OWNER APPROVAL** — organised as a **strategic cycle** and an **operational cycle**. **(f) THE WORKED RAIL EXAMPLE** — a System under Consideration partitioned into **Zone A "Network Gateways"**, **Zone B "Passenger Entertainment"** and **Zone C "Safety-critical Systems"**, with an attacker path running to a consequence; and a zoom into **Zone A showing an LTE modem, a SATELLITE modem and a "receiver for signalisation" behind a SECURITY GATEWAY**, which mediates flows "toward zone B (passenger entertainment)" and "toward zone C (safety-critical systems)". **(g) AUTOMATED SECURITY LEVEL TARGET (SL-T)** — computed from **unmitigated risk level** (from the risk assessment), **tolerable risk level** (a constant decided at context establishment) and **attacker strength** (a constant from the threat environment); "Security Level allocated at **Zone level and on each Asset**, based on **7 Foundational Requirements**" — **FR1 identification and authentication control · FR2 use control · FR3 system integrity · FR4 data confidentiality · FR5 restricted data flow · FR6 timely response to events · FR7 resource availability** — yielding "**a vector of SLs**" (worked example IAC 2, UC 2, SI 3, DC –, RDF 2, TRE 3, RA 2). Three observations: **(i)** the architecture runs the vehicle link over **GSM-R**, so oKMC is being introduced on the *legacy* bearer and will have to migrate with it — an R2 coexistence item and a concrete instance of the "new digital capability layered onto the old radio" pattern; **(ii)** it is deployed across **three geo-redundant sites (Karlsruhe, Duisburg, Hanover)**, which is R3's prescribed pattern in practice and worth citing as a domestic precedent for geo-redundancy in a safety-adjacent system; **(iii)** its **user interface sits in the CLOUD behind a firewall/VPN, with an HSM protecting ETCS keys** — i.e. a real instance of the safety-critical-to-cloud boundary that UITP/IEC 63452 Annex K addresses (E-2026-08-15-33) and that the Cloud4Rail thread debates (E-2026-07-02-27). **This is the closest thing on file to a worked German example of the cloud/vital interface, under regulator supervision.** **⑤ (f) IS A REGULATOR'S SUPERVISION CHECKLIST AND IS DIRECTLY REUSABLE.** Eighteen named focus areas — including **attack detection, logging, redundancy, vulnerability scan, penetration test, system hardening & cryptography, identity & access management, IT emergency, test & release** — constitute what EBA actually examines. **For ADR-012 (what a compliant estate must evidence) and ADR-007 (what the test programme must cover), this is a free, authoritative scope list from the very authority that would supervise the client.** Note that **attack detection and logging both appear**, which is the supervisory counterpart to the detection-maturity gap ENISA measured (E-2026-08-15-03/-16) and to R12's thesis. **⑥ (b) RESTATES THE COUPLING THIS ENGAGEMENT IS BUILT ON, FROM THE REGULATOR:** "**an integrated view of safety and cybersecurity is essential**", and "**to ensure safety, risks must remain at an acceptable level**". Combined with EBA's 2022 position that its safety mandate encompasses IT security (E-2026-08-15-11), Germany's regulator is consistently treating the two as one supervisory problem — the position ADR-012 and ADR-004 jointly assume, and the opposite of the French structural split (E-2026-08-15-35). **⑦ THE NSA-TO-NSA NETWORK AT (a) IS WORTH NOTING** — regular exchange with **BSI** plus **BAV (CH), EPSF (FR), NSA Rail Belgium, SJT (NO) and Traficom (FI)**. The register has now logged four of those authorities directly; this confirms they operate as a working peer group, which matters for the cross-border assurance-divergence concern raised at E-2026-08-15-35. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** **R3 stays "Strengthened post-incident — open"** — this adds a current, regulator-sourced instance of the SPOF concern but proves nothing by test, which is what ADR-007 must supply; **R4 unchanged**, with the 99.9%/9h datum recorded as calibration; R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed; R11/ADR-004 Proposed; R2/R5/R6 Accepted; R12 Proposed. No matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UPS, ranked:** (1) **EDIS** — scope, architecture, and whether the central coupling-node redundancy concern was resolved; a national dispatch system with a regulator-flagged SPOF is materially relevant to R3 and to the client's own estate; (2) **oKMC** — its cloud/vital boundary design and its GSM-R→FRMCS migration path, as a domestic worked example for ADR-004 and R2; (3) **EBA's "approve security experts" scheme** — the concrete route, criteria and register, for ADR-004 action 5; (4) the **18 focus areas** in their fuller form, if EBA publishes them, as an ADR-007 scope baseline. Total 60%.** An infrastructure manager ingesting **700 billion logs a year across 900 TB through 640 pipelines** has achieved **one tenth** of its intended monitoring coverage **on the railway estate itself**. **The detection gap is therefore not a maturity abstraction or a survey artefact — it is an operator's own measured shortfall, and it is worst exactly where the safety-relevant systems are.** This converts a four-year, multi-source qualitative finding into a single hard figure: ENISA measured detection and log correlation as the low-maturity areas in 2020 (E-2026-08-15-03); attributed it to expertise and resources, "**even more pronounced for OT systems, managed more generally by IMs**", in 2021 (E-2026-08-15-06); reported "for the OT (safety related) ones, **there is a gap**" (E-2026-08-15-04); and its investment survey found detection skills the least funded of ten, with 28% of transport OES having no SOC at all (E-2026-08-15-16). **Infrabel is one of the operators that *does* have a SOC, and it is at 10% on railway infrastructure.** **② THE STATED CAUSE IS SUPPLIER DEPENDENCY, AND IT IS THE SAME MECHANISM THE REGISTER HAS TRACKED ELSEWHERE.** The railway line reads "**need to be restarted from the beginning with our suppliers…**", the roll-out slide says the remaining work is "with our **suppliers** and teams to deploy OT and Railway use cases", and the closing lesson is "**your suppliers are keys, but…**" — the ellipsis doing considerable work. **An IM cannot monitor equipment whose logs, interfaces and cooperation it does not control.** That is R8/PR13 (vendor opacity and fix-dependency) expressed as an observability failure, and it is the operational counterpart to the CRA's SBOM and vulnerability-handling duties (ADR-012 actions 1-2), to the NIS-2 "important entity" status of rail manufacturers (E-2026-08-15-18) and to the third-party-risk funding gap ENISA measured (86% policy / 47% budget / 24% role, E-2026-08-15-16). **Procurement is the lever: monitorability — log formats, feeds and access — must be a contractual requirement, not a hoped-for cooperation.** Recommend adding it explicitly to ADR-012 action 2 alongside SBOM and support-period terms. **③ (g) PUTS GSM-R AND ETCS INSIDE A CYBERSOC SCOPE — DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THIS ENGAGEMENT.** The monitored railway estate includes **700 GSM-R base stations, 32 ETCS L2 RBCs, 10,000 signals and 800 level crossings**. **This is the first evidence on file of an IM bringing its radio bearer and ERTMS estate into cyber monitoring at all** — and it is at 10% coverage. For the FRMCS transition the implication is direct and actionable: **the bearer's monitorability should be designed in from the start rather than retrofitted against suppliers later.** That is precisely the gap the register documented from the specification side, where FRMCS SRS §15 places monitoring out of scope and **§17.2 system monitoring is EMPTY** (E-2026-07-12-02), after ERA had delegated radio-device security into the FRMCS specs (E-2026-08-15-04). **Infrabel's 10% is what that specification gap looks like in an operations centre.** **④ (i) IS AN OUT-OF-BAND MONITORING ARCHITECTURE AND IT ALIGNS WITH ADR-004.** Logs leave **Zones «Railway»** through a **log collector → gateway → firewall → PAM → VPN** into Kafka/ELK in **Zone «Infrabel»**, where the CyberSOC consumes them; third-party probes and vendor solutions traverse the same controlled path. **That is telemetry egress from the vital estate to an analysis domain across a mediated boundary** — the same shape as ADR-004's unidirectional read path, and as the IEC 63452 Annex K rule that monitoring data from OT to a cloud instance "should be implemented in a uni-directional fashion" (E-2026-08-15-33). **A working operator instance of the boundary ADR-004 proposes, with PAM as the access-control mechanism — worth citing as design-basis precedent.** **⑤ (n) IS THE MOST USEFUL SET OF LESSONS FOR ANYONE BUILDING THIS.** "**Do not overlook the difficulty of collecting QUALITY logs**" is the practical form of the observability problem — quantity is not the constraint (700 billion logs) but *quality and coverage* are. "**Raise knowledge before starting**" and "**maturity in risk assessment → use cases on OT/Railway**" say the method must precede the tooling; note that Infrabel's use cases are derived from risk assessment, which connects to the ARAMIS/SL-T and 63452 risk-method threads (E-2026-08-15-34, -32). "**Don't deploy systems and only if this is really necessary**" is a restraint principle worth carrying into any oversight-layer design — every added system is added attack surface and added telemetry burden. **⑥ (k) AND (c) GIVE R12 ITS OPERATIONAL VOCABULARY:** **715 incidents in Q3 2025 with 36% escalated**, tracked against **MTTD/MTTR**, with outcomes classified **benign-true-positive / true-positive / false-positive**. **That is the quantitative shape an oversight layer's alerting must fit** — and the 36% escalation rate is a useful anchor for the automation-bias and alert-fatigue concerns in ADR-004/R10: roughly two thirds of incidents are resolved without escalation, so the human-in-command gate sees a filtered stream whose filtering is itself a trust dependency. **⑦ (a) AND (e) ARE GOVERNANCE DATA POINTS:** Infrabel created "**a division to manage Cyber Resilience**" under NIS2, and delivers the SOC through a **managed-services contract** rather than fully in-house — a different answer from SNCF's "internalization of penetration testing competencies" (E-2026-08-15-15) and worth setting beside it when advising on build-versus-buy for the capacity constraint. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** **R12 stays Proposed · ADR-002** — this is the strongest justification yet for the Risk Sentinel/Assurance layer, and it sharpens the design constraint (an oversight layer cannot assume a mature detection substrate; on the railway estate there may be almost none), but it decides nothing; R8 Recommended; R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed; R11/ADR-004 Proposed; R3/R4 unchanged. The first lever — using the **SERA directive's requirements-capture** route combined with NIS-2 to reach vehicles — is a legal technique worth understanding, since it is how ILT reached rolling stock at all; **the deck asserts it without explaining it, so the mechanism needs verification before it is relied on.** **③ (b)/(d) INTRODUCE "ACCEPTABLE MEANS OF COMPLIANCE" AS A REGULATORY DEVICE — AND THE AMC IS MONITORING.** Where full retrofit is infeasible, ILT accepts **passive network monitoring**, **IDS implementation during retrofit**, and physical-security compensations. **This is the same compensating-measures logic that CRSG applies to CRA scope (legacy kept "as is" if compensated, documented as SecRACs — E-2026-08-15-30) and that ESCG applies to ERTMS legacy (E-2026-08-15-19), now applied by a supervisor to rolling stock.** Three independent instances of one pattern: **where you cannot fix the component, instrument it and constrain it, and document the conditions.** That is also, notably, **an argument for observability as a regulatory answer, not merely an engineering one** — which strengthens R12's position considerably: monitoring is not just how you detect, it is how you become compliant when you cannot remediate. **④ (d)'s PHYSICAL-SECURITY AMC IS CHEAP, CONCRETE AND EASILY OVERLOOKED — "technical panels, doors, TOILETS".** On trains the technical cabinets are frequently in or adjacent to toilet and vestibule areas; controlling physical access to them is a low-cost compensating control against the on-board access vector. It pairs with SNCF's named rolling-stock attack surfaces — **wireless and MAINTENANCE ACCESS** (E-2026-08-15-15) — and with the Airbus/Alstom zone model where the gateway zone sits between bearer and vital systems (E-2026-08-15-34). **⑤ (e)1 IS THE EXACT PROBLEM INFRABEL REPORTED THE SAME DAY, NOW VOICED BY A REGULATOR.** ILT appeals for "**manufacturers figuring out monitoring rules/use cases**"; Infrabel reported **10% use-case coverage on railway infrastructure** with the note "**need to be restarted from the beginning with our suppliers**" and the lesson "your suppliers are keys, but…" (E-2026-08-15-39). **Operator and supervisor, at the same conference, identifying the same blocker: manufacturers have not defined monitoring use cases for their own equipment.** That is a strong, two-sided evidential base for making **monitorability a procurement requirement** (ADR-012 action 2) rather than a hoped-for cooperation — and it is the operational face of the FRMCS specification gap where §17.2 system monitoring is empty (E-2026-07-12-02). **⑥ (c) IS MODEST BUT REAL — ENFORCEMENT PRODUCED A DESIGN CHANGE.** "One RU changed designs of trains" is the only outcome claimed, and it is unverified — but it is the first evidence in this corpus that **supervisory pressure has actually altered rolling-stock design**, as against strategies, frameworks and working groups. The stated intention to "**add infrastructure (same legal construct)**" and to extend to **tram, metro and bus** indicates the technique is being generalised, and matches the urban-rail widening seen elsewhere (E-2026-08-15-38, -32). **⑦ THE SUPERVISORY POSTURE ITSELF IS THE CONTEXT SIGNAL:** a department titled **Cybersecurity Oversight** inside a transport inspectorate, with a **Senior Inspector NIS-directive**, presenting under the banner "**increasing the pressure**". Read with the Dutch NIS-2 transposition picture (E-2026-08-15-13, -22) and the German supervisory apparatus (E-2026-08-15-11, -36), **the direction of travel across Member States is from guidance to enforcement** — which is the environment ADR-012's conformance work has to land in. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** **R13 stays Open — external dependency · ADR-009**; R2 Accepted; R12 Proposed — though ③ materially strengthens its justification; R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed; R8 Recommended; R11/ADR-004 Proposed. Paraphrased: **(a) THREE CRA USE CASES FOR ROLLING STOCK** — "**greenfield development of components**" (start from scratch) · "**upgrading existing components**" (enhance existing systems) · "**railway retrofitting**" (adapt legacy trains). **(b) GREENFIELD — "the security lifecycle IN REALITY"**, presented as a wry four-stage degradation: "**sales promised SL3**" → "**how security understood requirements**" → "**security after budgeting**" → "**from a pentester's perspective**". *Key learnings*: "**verify that your hardware is designed for IEC 62443-4-2 SL3**" and "**execute security tests in a very early phase**". **(c) UPGRADING EXISTING COMPONENTS** — *key learnings*: "**prioritised strategy based on an IEC 62443-3-2 risk assessment**" and "**focus on evaluation criteria of IEC TS 62443-6-2**". **(d) THE TECHNICAL CORE — "product development according IEC 62443-4-2 and IEC TS 62443-6-2":** **IEC 62443-4-2** answers "**what shall be implemented?**" and requires of network protocols **confidentiality, integrity and authenticity**; but the **insecure OT protocols in use are named as CAN, MVB, WTB, TRDP and PROFINET**, prompting the question "**is it possible to achieve 4-2 conformity with these protocols?**"; **IEC TS 62443-6-2** answers "**how shall it be tested?**" and supplies the resolution — "**insecure fieldbus protocols CAN BE USED IF COMPENSATING COUNTERMEASURES ARE IMPLEMENTED**". **(e) RAILWAY RETROFITTING** — opens with the objection it must answer: "**why invest in cybersecurity for older trains? They've been operating safely for decades!**"; diagnoses the legacy baseline as a "**FLAT NETWORK ARCHITECTURE WITH DIRECT CONNECTION TO THE OPERATOR**"; and prescribes "**segment the network**", "**add a security gateway**", "**add an intrusion detection system**". **(f) MEASURES IN RETROFITTING PROJECTS**, split two ways: *technical* — **network segmentation, security gateway** — "**greatly improves security, but must be CLOSELY COORDINATED**"; *organizational* — **physical access control, intrusion detection systems** — "**less intrusive changes, but require NEW PROCESSES**". already runs.** **① (d) NAMES THE INSECURE TRAIN PROTOCOLS AND GIVES THE STANDARDS-SANCTIONED WAY AROUND THEM.** The on-board buses in service — **CAN, MVB (Multifunction Vehicle Bus), WTB (Wire Train Bus), TRDP (Train Real-time Data Protocol) and PROFINET** — offer none of the confidentiality, integrity or authenticity that **IEC 62443-4-2** requires of network protocols, so 4-2 conformity cannot be achieved through the protocols themselves. **IEC TS 62443-6-2's resolution is that insecure fieldbus protocols may still be used where COMPENSATING COUNTERMEASURES are implemented.** The register already carried this problem in general terms — a 2024 MDPI review flagged the "legacy MVB/CAN integration gap" (E-2026-07-29-11) — **but this names the full protocol set and, more usefully, supplies the standards route by which a non-conformant bus can remain in service.** That matters for **R13/R2** because it means **the on-board legacy bus estate does not have to be replaced to reach conformity**, which is the difference between a feasible and an infeasible retrofit programme. **② AND IT IS THE FOURTH INDEPENDENT INSTANCE OF ONE PATTERN — "compensate and document".** CRSG applies it to CRA scope, keeping legacy components "as is" where compensated, recorded as **SecRACs** (E-2026-08-15-30); ESCG applies it to ERTMS legacy with per-phase risk analysis (E-2026-08-15-19); **ILT applies it as a supervisor, accepting passive monitoring and IDS as Acceptable Means of Compliance** (E-2026-08-15-40); and here **IEC TS 62443-6-2 applies it to insecure fieldbus protocols**. **Four different regimes — product regulation, sector standard, national supervision and industrial-security standard — converging on the same mechanism: where the component cannot be made conformant, constrain and instrument it, and document the conditions.** That is now a well-evidenced sector principle and should be stated as such in ADR-012, and echoed in ADR-004's treatment of conditions under which an argument holds. **③ (e)'s "FLAT NETWORK ARCHITECTURE WITH DIRECT CONNECTION TO THE OPERATOR" IS THE LEGACY BASELINE THE REGISTER HAS LACKED IN PLAIN TERMS.** It explains why on-board segmentation matters and why the prescribed remedies — **segment, add a security gateway, add an IDS** — recur across every rolling-stock artefact on file: SNCF's zones-and-conduits practice with wireless and maintenance access as the named surfaces (E-2026-08-15-15), the Airbus/Alstom worked zone model with LTE and satellite modems behind a security gateway (E-2026-08-15-34), SUBSET-147's mandated on-board zoning separating the FRMCS zone from CCS (E-2026-08-01-14), and ILT's AMC list (E-2026-08-15-40). **For the FRMCS onboard segment the implication is the same one this register keeps reaching: the bearer must land behind a gateway in a segmented consist network, not on a flat bus with a path to the operator.** **④ (b) IS A VENDOR MAKING A POINT THAT SUPPORTS A PROCUREMENT POSITION.** The four-stage decline from "**sales promised SL3**" to "from a **pentester's** perspective" is self-serving — a pentest firm arguing that claimed security levels do not survive testing — **but it is the same argument the register has reached from the regulatory side**: tmc noted that "for most products a **self-assessment** confirms CRA compliancy" (E-2026-08-15-29), and the Swedish deck placed **control systems and crypto HSM/KMS in CRA Annex IV requiring third-party assessment** (E-2026-08-15-38). **A supplier's declared Security Level is a claim, not a verified property** — which is precisely why ADR-012 action 2 should state whether the engagement accepts self-declaration or requires independent assessment, and why "**execute security tests in a very early phase**" is sound advice for ADR-007's test surfaces. **⑤ (a)'s THREE USE CASES ARE A USEFUL TAXONOMY** and map cleanly onto CRSG's CRA progressivity model — greenfield ≈ "compliant by design", upgrading ≈ "new baseline", retrofitting ≈ "used as is with mitigating measures and conditions of use" (E-2026-08-15-30). **The engagement's FRMCS programme spans all three simultaneously**, which is worth saying plainly: new FRMCS components are greenfield, the CCS estate they attach to is being upgraded, and the existing fleet is retrofit — three different compliance postures inside one programme, on top of the December-2027 individual-product boundary (E-2026-08-15-28). **⑥ (f)'s HONEST TRADE-OFF IS WORTH CARRYING:** segmentation and gateways "greatly improve security **but must be closely coordinated**" (i.e. they touch the vehicle's functional architecture and its approval), whereas physical access control and monitoring are "**less intrusive… but require new processes**" (i.e. they shift cost from engineering to operations). **That is the retrofit economics question R13 turns on, stated compactly.** **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R13 stays Open — external dependency · ADR-009; R2 Accepted; R11/ADR-004 and R12 Proposed; R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed. No matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UPS:** (1) **IEC TS 62443-6-2** — the compensating-countermeasures evaluation criteria for insecure fieldbus protocols; if it is obtainable it is directly useful to R13 and to any FRMCS on-board security case, and it is not on file; (2) whether **TRDP/MVB/WTB** security is addressed anywhere in the UNISIG/SUBSET-147 consist-network work already logged, or left entirely to compensating measures; (3) IEC 62443-3-2 as the risk-assessment method referenced here and by ARAMIS (E-2026-08-15-34) — a recurring anchor worth holding directly. No TLP marking observed | A (primary — RNE describing RNE's own platform, membership and ISMS, by its CIO; **THREE FLAGS**: **self-reported** with no assurance evidence (ISO 27001 conformity is stated as an aim — "shall be fully aligned" — not as a certification held); **slide-deck**, several slides unread images; **information-layer scope** — the CI and TIS are planning, allocation and train-information systems, **not** the operational control or bearer layer, so relevance to FRMCS is indirect) | R7 interoperability (+ **R3/R4 European concentration point**; R14/ADR-012 ISMS & PKI; R12 monitoring) | validate | **A, moderate value — the information layer rather than the operational one, but it contributes two things the register should hold.** **① IT IDENTIFIES A PAN-EUROPEAN CONCENTRATION POINT: RNE IS THE CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY FOR THE COMMON INTERFACE, AND NEARLY ALL EUROPEAN IMs AND ALLOCATION BODIES USE IT.** "All certificates are issued and managed by RNE to ensure trust across the rail network", and "RNE acts as Certificate Authority for CI". **That is a single trust anchor underneath the cross-border capacity-request, timetabling and train-information exchange of almost every European infrastructure manager.** For **R3** — "eliminate the central single point of failure" — this is a different *kind* of central point from the one the 23-June outage exposed (that was a national bearer/core; this is a European trust and data-exchange service), but it is a concentration nonetheless, and the register should record it as such. Loss or compromise of the CI trust chain would not stop trains directly — the CI is an information system, not a control system — **but per RNE's own framing it "protects continuity of critical European rail coordination"**, so degradation would impair cross-border path allocation and train information. **Worth noting alongside the other shared-dependency findings and worth asking about: what is RNE's CA continuity and compromise-recovery posture?** **② ERA TECHNICAL DOCUMENT 104 IS NEW TO THIS REGISTER** (zero prior occurrences), and it is the ERA instrument governing **CI message signing**. Together with the mutual-TLS and PKI construction at (d) it means the **information layer already has a mandated, ERA-referenced application-security scheme** — which is a useful contrast to draw: **the message-exchange layer has ERA-specified signing and a working PKI, while the operational layer's cybersecurity requirements in the TSIs are, per the ERTMS Users Group and two national NSAs, absent or scoped only to cross-border interoperability** (E-2026-08-15-19, -10, -35). **The sector has better-specified security for timetable messages than for the systems that move trains.** That is a sharp, defensible observation for client material, and it is grounded entirely in primary sources already on file. **③ (g) IS THE MOST QUIETLY REVEALING SLIDE: RNE'S ISO 27001 IMPACT SCALE IS DENOMINATED PURELY IN EUROS**, topping out at "> €4 million", with **no safety, service-continuity or societal dimension at any tier**. For an ISMS covering systems that coordinate European rail capacity, impact is measured only as financial loss. **This is the safety/security and IT/OT divide showing up inside a risk matrix** — and it contrasts directly with the rail-safety regime the register already holds, where CSM-RA harmonised design targets are consequence-based (10⁻⁹/h catastrophic, 10⁻⁷/h critical, E-2026-07-07-02) and severity is fatality-anchored. **It is a concrete instance of the problem ENISA named as "reconciling safety and cybersecurity worlds" (E-2026-08-15-07) and that UITP's determinism argument attacks from the other side (E-2026-08-15-33).** Not a criticism of RNE — an information-exchange body may reasonably scope impact financially — but **a caution the engagement should carry: an ISO 27001 ISMS imported wholesale into a safety-relevant context will measure the wrong thing unless its impact scale is extended.** Directly relevant to ADR-012, which must couple security management to a safety case rather than run alongside it. **④ (a) IS THE FRAGMENTATION THEME AGAIN, IN A FOURTH DOMAIN.** "Isolated with a national focus", "cooperation islands", "varying levels of maturity and digitalization", "request country by country for a single train run" — the register has now documented European rail fragmentation in **supervisory competence** (FR/DE/FI/BE), **technical specification** (TSI subsets scoped to RBC-Euroradio, per-operator security solutions), **supplier practice** (Alstom's EBIOS/62443/TS 50701 mix) and now **capacity-management IT**. That consistency is worth stating: **fragmentation is not a cybersecurity problem the sector happens to have; it is the sector's structural condition, and cybersecurity inherits it.** **⑤ (f) IS A CONVENTIONAL BUT USABLE ISMS RISK PROCESS** — asset classification, threat sources and BIA feeding a 4×4 likelihood-impact matrix with avoid/reduce/share/accept treatment and **quarterly monitoring reports**. Unremarkable in itself, but it is the fourth risk-method on file (with ARAMIS/EBIOS-RM+62443 at E-2026-08-15-34, IEC 62443-3-2 at E-2026-08-15-41, and the ENISA SCSA method at E-2026-08-15-08) — **another instance of method proliferation, and a reminder that ADR-012 should choose and justify one rather than inherit whichever arrives with a supplier.** **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R7 stays Accepted; R3/R4 unchanged — the CA concentration is recorded as an observation, not a status change; R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed; R12 Proposed. No matrix change, no ADR change. **FOLLOW-UPS:** (1) **ERA Technical Document 104** — the message-signing provisions, as a primary and as the contrast case for the operational-layer gap; (2) **RNE's CA continuity and compromise posture** — a European single trust anchor deserves the same scrutiny the register applies to other central points; (3) whether the **Telematics TSI** (TAF/TAP) carries cybersecurity requirements the CCS TSI lacks — ERA said in 2020 that IT security would be included in TAF/TAP, OPE and CCS (E-2026-08-15-02), and this deck suggests TAF/TAP-side security is comparatively developed. Paraphrased: **(a) RAILWAY SAFETY CULTURE** — the **European Safety Culture Model 2.0**, built from **Cultural Enablers** ("levers through which an organisational culture develops"), **Behaviour Patterns** ("shared ways of thinking and acting which convey the organisational culture") and **Railway Safety Fundamentals** ("core principles which must be reflected by behaviour patterns to achieve sustainable safety performance"); delivered through a **Safety Culture Programme** "to devise dissemination and evaluation instruments… within the Single European Railway Area", whose key principle is that "**any deliverable is tested with partner organisations**". **(b) ORGANISATIONAL JUST CULTURE (OJC)** — developed through "dedication and consistency", "**open and respectful dialogue (staff report safety issues)**" and "analyse and act upon to improve", to achieve "appropriate, sustainable, safe operational performance"; supported by a **free online basic module** and the **ERA Just Culture Flow** cycle (search for inputs → initialise understanding and care → explore operational reasoning → explore system influences → decide and implement → disseminate outcomes and monitor). **(c) SMS AND THE RU-IM INTERFACE** — the SMS is "the organisation, arrangements and procedures established by an IM or an RU to ensure the safe management of its operations", with **RUs and IMs each responsible for their own part**; "**RUs [and] IMs shall co-operate together to manage the INTERFACE RISKS**", demonstrating through their SMS the ability to identify, assess and control "risks which arise from its own activities **and risks caused by others**"; and the **NSA "has still the ability to check effectively the co-operation arrangements put in place by RUs [and] IMs during its supervision activities"**. On the risk-based approach: "**new/amended rules shall be traced back to the original identified risk**", but "**difficult to relate numerous old rules to risks. There is no single solution**". **(d) SIGNIFICANT CHANGE — Reg (EU) 402/2013** — its criteria for assessing the significance of a safety-related change require "adequate documentation to justify the decision"; "**the question on the significance of a safety-related change does NOT release the railway company from its obligation to perform a proper risk assessment**" demonstrating that safety "is maintained or even improved"; and "**when the change is significant, in addition to the RA, an INDEPENDENT ASSESSMENT BODY must be appointed, to verify independently the correct application of the RA — Annex I Reg. 402-2013**". **(e) CYBERTHREAT IN RAILWAY — the slide that matters most here:** "**'Cyber' risks CANNOT BE DISSOCIATED from railway risks**"; "**Boundary between railway safety and cybersecurity TO BE DETERMINED…**"; "**essential to clarify the functioning at the INTERFACE between the 'worlds' SMS – IMS**"; "the increasing degree of connectivity of the infrastructure and rolling stock (i.e. **DAC – FDFTO**) is creating a **significant increase of their attack surface**"; and "**programmable devices [are] exposed to cyberthreats when 'NOT CONNECTED' — besides communication, we need to protect design, production, maintenance (standards, certifications…)**". **(f) WHAT TO HIGHLIGHT** — the respective scopes of the railway and cybersecurity regulatory frameworks; "**ongoing works aiming to build a SHARED FRAMEWORK between safety and cybersecurity**"; operational subjects justifying "the need for a clear operating framework in the area of '**overall' safety**"; and recommendations from the discussions. **(g) REGULATORY FRAMEWORKS — "terms & competences are different":** *railway safety* = "overall functioning of the system, subsystems (INF, RST, CCS, OPE…)", where "the risks are above all, technical and environmental"; *operating safety* = the ability of components (brakes, etc.) to meet their functions; *cybersecurity* = protecting networks, computers and data against attacks, damage and unauthorised access; and "**IT 'security' includes cybersecurity & physical safety**". Standards named: **IEC 62443**, **CLC/TS 50701**, and **IEC 63452** — described in the future tense as a standard that "**aims to create** a strong, clear, and implementable framework… across rolling stock, fixed installations, management systems and additional services". **(h) IMPLEMENT AND SHARE** — the **ENISA & ER-ISAC report "Building cyber secure Railway Infrastructure" (2022)**, on "sectorial implementation of the NIS Directive"; and the **ENISA Transport Threat Landscape** mapping cyber incidents 2021-2022 across aviation, maritime, railway and road. **(i) THE LINK, in five dimensions, each mapped to named Safety Culture Model elements:** *risk management perspective* → **F1.1 risk awareness, F1.3 questioning attitude**; *organisational awareness and training* → E2.3 organisational systems, **E3.2 competence management**, F2.2 system complexity; *resilience and incident response* → **F1.2 resilience, F2.3 reporting, F3.2 analysis, F3.3 learning from others (cross-sector mitigation)**; *regulatory compliance* → E2.1 roles and responsibilities, E2.2 organisational design, E2.3 organisational systems, E1.3 regulatory relationships — noting an "**area of potential conflict, transparency vs privacy**"; *cultural norms and organisational values* → E1.1 teamwork and collaboration, E1.2 interpersonal values, **E4.1 leading by example, F4.3 decision making**. **(j) RESOURCES** — ERA guides on safety culture, TSI OPE, **human and organisational factors (HOF)**, CSM on SMS, and single safety certificate applications. Five points are directly usable.** **① A FIFTH NATIONAL COMPETENCE MODEL, AND THE RAIL NSA IS ABSENT FROM IT.** Belgium splits the job between the **CCB** — national cyber authority, national CSIRT, SPOC and supervisor of essential/important entities — and a **transport sectoral authority, the FPS Mobility and Transport**, which holds identification, sectoral exercises, additional risk-management measures, inspection and **administrative fines**. **The rail safety authority does not appear.** Set against the models already on file — **FR** (EPSF has no cyber competence; ANSSI has no rail mandate), **DE** (EBA reads its safety mandate as including IT security and approves security experts), **FI** (one agency holds NSA, NIS competent authority and CERT) — **Belgium places sectoral cyber supervision with the transport MINISTRY rather than the rail regulator.** That is a fourth distinct arrangement and it reinforces the register's finding that **national supervisory competence for rail cybersecurity diverges structurally across the Union** (E-2026-08-15-35, -11, -12) — a live cross-border assurance problem. **② "NIS2 SCOPE = WHOLE ENTITY" IS A SCOPING POINT ADR-012 SHOULD STATE EXPLICITLY.** The deck is emphatic and illustrates it with a smart coffee machine alongside company servers: the obligations attach to the **entire entity**, not to a carved-out set of critical systems. For an infrastructure manager that means corporate IT, office estate and OT alike. **ADR-012 currently frames NIS-2 as operator-side risk management and incident reporting; it does not say that the perimeter is the whole organisation.** Worth making explicit, because it materially changes the scale of the compliance surface — and it contrasts with the CRA, which attaches per product. **③ (h) IS THE SUPPLY-CHAIN FLOW-DOWN MECHANISM — AND A NATIONAL AUTHORITY CONCEDING ITS UNDER-SPECIFICATION.** NIS-2 obliges the entity to **impose** risk-management measures on direct suppliers and to **control respect** of them, reaching suppliers that are themselves **not NIS-2 entities** — but "**the NIS2 law… does not state HOW it should be achieved**". **That is exactly the gap ADR-012 action 2 fills with contractual terms**, and it is now supported by a national supervisor's own statement that the law leaves the method open. Belgium's answer is to recommend a framework (CyFun); **the engagement's answer should be contractual clauses** — and this row is the legal-basis evidence for insisting on them. It also connects to Infrabel's finding, from the same country, that supplier cooperation is the binding constraint on monitoring coverage (E-2026-08-15-39) and to ILT's appeal for manufacturers to define monitoring use cases (E-2026-08-15-40). **④ THE FINES ARE NEW TO THE REGISTER AND BELONG BESIDE THE CRA FIGURES.** ADR-012's legal basis records **CRA Art 64 at €15M / 2.5%**; the NIS-2 exposure is now documented at **€10M or 2% of worldwide turnover for essential entities** and **€7M or 1.4% for important entities**, doubled for repetition within three years — plus non-monetary powers that matter more in practice: **suspension of a certification or authorisation** and **temporary prohibition on exercising managerial functions**, both for essential entities. **For a client conversation about why ADR-012 is not optional, the ability to suspend an authorisation and to bar managers is a sharper argument than the fine ceiling.** Note also the **€200 000 penalty for sanctioning an employee or subcontractor who performed NIS-2 obligations in good faith** — a protection for those who report, which is the legal counterpart to the Organisational Just Culture that R12's evidence chain depends on (E-2026-08-15-43). **⑤ (j)'s DIFFERENTIATED SUPERVISION AND (d)'s PRESUMPTION OF CONFORMITY GIVE ADR-012 A COMPLIANCE ROUTE.** Essential entities face **ex-ante as well as ex-post** supervision and **must** undergo regular conformity assessment — via **CyFun or ISO 27001 certification by an accredited CAB**, which confers **presumption of conformity**, or else a **CCB inspection at the entity's own cost**. **That is the same "standards deliverables → presumption of conformity" architecture the register has now seen from three other directions** — EPSF's proposed chain of TS 50701/IEC 63452 → CRA → NIS-2 (E-2026-08-15-35), CENELEC WG 26's forthcoming IEC 63452 European Annex (E-2026-08-15-32) and CRSG's sector guidance (E-2026-08-15-30). **The consistent lesson for ADR-012: certification against a recognised framework is the practical route to demonstrating conformance, and the engagement should choose its framework deliberately rather than inherit one.** **⑥ (i)'s FINAL-REPORT REQUIREMENT IS POINTED FOR THIS ENGAGEMENT:** within one month, the entity must state "**the type of threat or ROOT CAUSE that likely triggered the incident**". The 23-June 2026 outage's root cause — a planned component swap triggering a silent software fault so failover never engaged — took days to establish publicly (E-2026-06-27-01/-03). **A one-month statutory root-cause deadline is a real operational requirement on the diagnostic capability R12 exists to provide**, and it is worth noting that the same regime requires the 24-hour early warning to state whether the cause is *presumed malicious* — a determination the Dutch and French authorities have both said is not a solved process (E-2026-08-15-10). **⑦ MINOR BUT WORTH RECORDING: the Commission Implementing Act specifying risk-management measures and significant-incident thresholds covers DIGITAL sectors only, not transport** (a). So rail has **no EU-level implementing specification** of its NIS-2 measures — the detail is left to national law and sectoral authorities, which is precisely the mechanism by which the divergence at ① arises. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R14 stays Open (ADR-012 Proposed); R8 Recommended; R12/R10 Proposed; R3/R4 unchanged. ADR-004 exists precisely to ensure the learning components cannot become a risk factor for the safety case. **Having the SRG articulate the same concern — in 2024, before the engagement's own framing — is useful external validation that the guardrail is the right one to build the architecture around**, and it is quotable to a client audience that includes national ministries. **② (e)'s SECOND REQUIREMENT IS R4, STATED MORE RADICALLY THAN THE REGISTER HAS IT — AND IT CARRIES A REAL TENSION WORTH NAMING.** "**Critical safety on-board and ground systems should be implemented in a way that allows for them to be CIRCUMVENTED in the case of a cyber threat**", and "**redundancy needs to be ensured in 'crisis mode' with MINIMAL IT SUPPORT**". The second half is straightforwardly R4 — fail-soft, degraded mode, and notably a **degraded mode whose defining property is minimal IT dependency**, which is a sharper formulation than "multi-bearer fallback" and closer to what the 23-June outage actually demanded (manual recovery, local working). **But the first half deserves careful handling: a safety system designed to be circumventable under cyber threat is, by construction, a system with a bypass path — and a bypass path is an attack surface.** The Member States' requirement (an intervention route that survives a cyber event) is in direct tension with the security requirement (no unauthorised bypass), and **resolving that tension is exactly what ADR-004's design does**: a unidirectional boundary with human-in-command interposition means the *human* can act when the automation cannot be trusted, without creating a machine-reachable bypass. **Recommend ADR-004 address this explicitly** — it is the strongest policy-side argument for the human-in-command gate, and it also connects to Thron's observation that operator privileges must be sufficient to act in a degraded mode (E-2026-08-15-44). **③ (a)'s "IS THERE A NEED FOR A NEW CYBER SECURITY TSI?" IS THE MEMBER-STATES-SIDE VERSION OF THE TSI GAP THE REGISTER HAS DOCUMENTED FROM THREE OTHER DIRECTIONS.** The ERTMS Users Group established that the CCS TSI subsets' security scope is confined to cross-border interoperability (RBC-Euroradio) and sits below commonly agreed standards (E-2026-08-15-19); EPSF stated in 2022 and again in 2025 that the TSIs and CSMs carry "no explicit requirement for cybersecurity" (E-2026-08-15-10, -35); ERA's own intent to reflect security in the TSIs has been unchanged since 2019 (E-2026-08-15-02, -46). **Here the Member States ask whether a dedicated cybersecurity TSI is needed at all.** That is a distinct policy option the register had not recorded — neither ERA nor the sector bodies have proposed a *separate* TSI — and it is worth tracking, because a cybersecurity TSI would change the instrument landscape ADR-012 assumes. **④ (b)'s "REGULATION BETTER THAN DIRECTIVE BECAUSE OF INTEROPERABILITY" DIAGNOSES THE FRAGMENTATION'S LEGAL CAUSE.** The register has now documented divergence in supervisory competence (FR/DE/FI/BE — E-2026-08-15-35, -11, -12, -49), in technical specification (per-operator security solutions, E-2026-08-15-19), in supplier practice (E-2026-08-15-34) and in capacity-management IT (E-2026-08-15-42). **A Member State representative here names the mechanism: a Directive is transposed twenty-seven ways, and for an interoperable system that is itself the problem.** Belgium's own transposition deck illustrates the point precisely — national law, a national framework (CyFun), a national sectoral authority and national fines (E-2026-08-15-49). **This is a clean, citable articulation of why rail cyber governance fragments, and it is worth carrying into any client discussion of cross-border assurance.** **⑤ (c) CONNECTS THE SPACE/GNSS THREAD TO RAIL AT POLICY LEVEL — and it is the earliest such connection on file.** Naming **Galileo, EGNOS and GOVSATCOM** alongside a slide titled "impact of space technologies used in digitalization and automation of the rail system to cyber security" places satellite dependency in the rail cyber picture in **October 2024**, more than a year before the Estonian minister's GNSS-jamming warning that opened this gap in the register (E-2026-08-15-24). **The gap flagged there — that GNSS appears in this register only as a surveying tool, never as a jammable dependency — is therefore not merely an oversight but a live sector topic the register had missed.** The relevant slide is an unread image; **worth re-rendering if the GNSS-denial follow-up is pursued.** **⑥ (e)'s STRATEGIC FRAMING IS THE THIRD MILITARY-MOBILITY INSTANCE AND THE EARLIEST.** "Rail transport is a key strategic sector which must ensure the operation of other key sectors at all circumstances… **defence**, national internal security, the integrated rescue system and strategic industries" — together with the "**military and RID**" freight slide. The register recorded this framing from Estonia and Finland at the 5th conference (E-2026-08-15-24, -27); **this shows it present at Member-States level a year earlier**, which strengthens the case that defence readiness is a durable third justification for R3/R4 alongside safety and economic continuity. **⑦ (d) IS A BREADTH ARGUMENT** — cybersecurity spanning rolling-stock production through signalling and control to ticketing and consignment notes, mapped onto TSIs, **Reg (EU) 2020/1056** and the CIV/RID/CIM instruments — consistent with the "whole entity" scoping the Belgian authority gave NIS-2 (E-2026-08-15-49) and a reminder that the regulated surface reaches well beyond the CCS estate. **DOES NOT MOVE A DECISION:** R3 stays "Strengthened post-incident — open", R4 Open — **(e) restates them at policy level but proves nothing**; R9/R10/R11 Proposed; R7 Accepted — the cybersecurity-TSI question is recorded as a policy option, not a change; R14 Open, ADR-012 Proposed. No matrix change, no ADR change — **though ADR-004 has a specific item to address (the circumventability-versus-bypass tension at ②)**, offered not made. **FOLLOW-UPS:** (1) **re-render the six unread image slides**, particularly "impact of space technologies…" and "interoperability framework… (incl. telematics as non-safety related TSI)"; (2) whether the **cybersecurity-TSI question** has been taken up anywhere since — it did not appear at the 5th conference; (3) the **SRG's own outputs** on cybersecurity, if any are published. Note the strategic-autonomy condition: deployments "must be protected against possible dependencies and vulnerabilities... to **pre-empt foreign influence and control**" — the same policy instinct that drives **R8**, expressed as a funding condition. **(e) HORIZON EUROPE — TWO TOPICS, AND ONE OF THEM CORROBORATES AN EXISTING REGISTER THREAD RATHER THAN OPENING ONE.** **CL3-2024-CS-01-01** (IA, **€37M**, 6 projects): security in hardware/software development and assessment — "testing of hardware and software in **virtual, closed and secure environments**", automated vulnerability discovery and **dynamic security assessment**, "**trustworthy certifiable hardware and software**", AI-based predictive security and intrusion detection. Feeds **ADR-007 item 7** (design-stage/digital-twin testing) and touches **ADR-004** (certifiability). **CL3-2024-CS-01-02** (RIA, **€23.4M**, 4 projects): **post-quantum cryptography transition** — algorithm maturity, hybrid pre-/post-quantum transition tools, phase-in to existing applications, demonstrators. **⚠️ I initially drafted this as a gap in the register and that was WRONG — I checked before writing: PQC is an ESTABLISHED thread here (harvest-now-decrypt-later on long-lived signalling traffic, crypto-agility, NIST FIPS 203/204/205, the AES-128-lifespan procurement flag). This deck therefore CORROBORATES that thread with an institutional anchor — the EU funded the PQC transition at research level in 2024 — and does not surface anything new. The narrow open question it does raise: did any of those 4 projects produce rail-relevant output?** **(f) INSTITUTIONAL FACTS WORTH HAVING ON FILE** — ECCC established by **Reg (EU) 2021/887** (20.05.2021); **financially autonomous since 24.09.2024**; seated at the Polytechnic University of Bucharest (operations from 09.05.2023, permanent premises inaugurated 30.10.2024); ~38 staff. Three-part structure: **ECCC + Network of National Coordination Centres (one NCC per Member State, may receive AND pass on financial support) + the Cybersecurity Competence Community**. Leaders **EL 105 · RO 76 · CY 56 · BE 52 · IT 44**, against **DE 35 · FR 31 · ES 27 · NL 15**; **HU 0 coordinators**. Types: **50% private for-profit, 22% research & technology, 12% higher/secondary education, 8% public bodies, 8% other; 39% SME**.
